title: A prayer for words that uproot and plant
english: In the three books before this one, holy Ambrose, we have gone through what occurred to us in reply to Celsus’s treatise. Now, having prayed to God through Christ, we dictate a fourth in reply to what comes next. May we be given words such as those of which it is written in Jeremiah, where the Lord says to the prophet: “Behold, I have put my words into your mouth as fire. Behold, I have set you this day over nations and kingdoms, to root out and to dig down, to destroy and to pull down, to build again and to plant” (Jeremiah 1:9–10; 5:14).

For we too now need words that will root out whatever stands against the truth from every soul that has been harmed by Celsus’s treatise or by thoughts like his. We need thoughts as well that will dig down the buildings of every false opinion, and the building Celsus has put up in his treatise, which is like the building of those who said, “Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower whose top shall reach to heaven” (Genesis 11:4). And we need wisdom that pulls down every height that is lifted up “against the knowledge of God” (2 Corinthians 10:5), and the “height” of arrogance that Celsus has “lifted up” against us.

Then, since we must not stop at “rooting out and digging down” what we have named, but must “plant” a planting of God’s field in the ground of what has been rooted out, and must build God’s building and a temple of God’s glory in the place of what has been dug down (1 Corinthians 3:9), for this reason we too must pray to the Lord who gave what is written in Jeremiah, that he may give us also words for building up the things of Christ, and for “planting” the spiritual law and the prophetic words that answer to it.

Above all, in answer to what Celsus says next after the passages already treated, we need to establish that what was prophesied about Christ was rightly prophesied. For Celsus stands against both parties at once: against the Jews, who deny that the coming of Christ has taken place but hope that it will, and against the Christians, who confess that Jesus is the Christ who was prophesied. He says:

title: Celsus names no prophecy
english: “That some of the Christians, and the Jews, say, the former that some god or son of a god has come down to the earth as judge of the things here, the latter that he will come down, is most shameful, and its refutation does not even need a long argument.”

And here he does seem to speak with precision. Of the Jews he says, not of some but of all, that they think someone will come down to the earth; but of the Christians, that some of them say he has come down. For he is pointing to those who show from the Jewish Scriptures that the coming of Christ has already taken place, and he seems to know that there are some sects which deny that Christ Jesus is the one who was prophesied.

We have already treated in the earlier books, as far as we were able, the fact that Christ was prophesied; so we do not take up again most of what could be said on the subject, so as not to repeat ourselves. But notice this: if he wanted, with an argument that at least seemed to hold together, to overturn faith in the prophecies, or faith that Christ will come or has come, he ought to have set out the very prophecies that we Christians and Jews use when we debate with each other. In that way he might at least have seemed to draw those who are swayed by their persuasiveness, as he regards it, away from their assent to the prophetic writings and from the faith in Jesus as the Christ that comes to them through those writings.

As it is, either because he cannot answer the prophecies about Christ, or because he does not even know in the first place what the things prophesied about him are, he sets down not a single prophetic saying, though there are countless ones about Christ; and yet he thinks he can accuse the prophetic writings without even setting out what he himself would call their persuasiveness. He does not know, however, that the Jews by no means say that the Christ will come down as God, or as Son of God, as we have also said above.

title: What the descent was for
english: Having said that we claim he has come down, and the Jews that he will come down as judge, he thinks he condemns the claim on the spot as most shameful and in need of no long refutation, and he says: “What would be God’s purpose in such a descent?” He does not see that in our teaching too the descent has a purpose. In the first place, it was to turn back those whom the Gospel calls “the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24; 10:6). In the second place, because of their disobedience, it was to take from them what is called the kingdom of God (Matthew 21:43) and to give it “to other tenants,” to the Christians, as distinct from the Jews of old, who “will render” to God “the fruits” of the kingdom of God “in their seasons” (Matthew 21:41), each action being a fruit of the kingdom.

Out of many answers, then, we have given a few to Celsus’s question when he said: “What, then, would be God’s purpose in such a descent?” But Celsus puts forward for himself things that neither the Jews nor we would say, when he asks: “Or is it to learn what goes on among men?” For none of us says that Christ came into human life in order to learn what goes on among men. Then, as though some would say “to learn what goes on among men,” he raises against himself, in reply to this, the objection: “Does he not know all things?” Then, as though they would answer that he does know, he raises a further difficulty: “Does he know, then, and yet not set things right, and is he not able to set them right by divine power?”

All this he says naively. For God always sets right those who listen to what is said, by his own Word, who in every generation passes into holy souls and makes them friends of God and prophets (Wisdom of Solomon 7:27). And at the coming of Christ too he sets right, by the word of the Christian faith, not those who are unwilling, but those who have chosen the better life, the life pleasing to God.

I do not know what sort of correction Celsus wanted to take place when he raised the difficulty: “Is he not able to set things right by divine power, unless he sends someone by way of nature for this purpose?” Did he, then, want the correction to come about by impressions put into men’s minds by God, God taking away their vice all at once and planting virtue in them? Another may inquire whether such a thing is consistent with nature, or possible for it. But we would say: let it be so, and let it be possible. Where, then, is what lies in our power? And where is praiseworthy assent to the truth, or acceptable refusal of falsehood?

And even if it were once granted that this is both possible and fittingly done, why should one not rather raise the question at the very start, saying something like what Celsus says: could God not by divine power have made men who did not even need correction, but were good and perfect from the outset, with vice never having existed at all? Such arguments can carry away the untrained and the unintelligent, but not one who looks into the nature of things; for if you take away the voluntary character of virtue, you have taken away its very being as well.

These matters need a whole treatise. The Greeks too have said a good deal about them in their works On Providence, and they would not have said what Celsus set out when he said: “He knows, but does not set things right, nor is he able to set them right by divine power.” We ourselves have spoken of these questions in many places, as far as we could, and the divine words have made them plain to those who are able to hear them.

title: The same question falls on Celsus
english: So what Celsus brings against us and the Jews shall be said to him as well: Well, my good man, does the God who is over all know what goes on among men, or does he not know? If you hold that there is a God and a providence, as your treatise shows, he must know. And if he knows, why does he not set things right? Or are we obliged to give an account of why, knowing, he does not set things right, while you, who in your treatise do not altogether show yourself an Epicurean but profess to acknowledge providence, are not to be asked the same: why God, knowing all that goes on among men, does not set things right, nor by divine power free all men from vice?

But we are not ashamed to say that God always sends those who are to set things right; for the words that call men to what is best are present among men, since God has given them. Yet among those who serve God there are many differences, and few are those who uphold the truth wholly and purely and bring about complete correction, such as Moses and the prophets were. But beyond all these, great is the correction brought through Jesus, who did not wish only those in one corner of the world to be healed, but, as far as it lay with him, those everywhere; for he came as “Savior of all men” (1 Timothy 4:10).

title: God does not leave his seat
english: After this the most noble Celsus, taking it from I know not where, raises a difficulty against us, as though we said that God himself comes down to men; and he thinks it follows from this that he leaves his own seat. For he does not know the power of God, nor that “the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and that which holds all things together has knowledge of what is spoken” (Wisdom of Solomon 1:7). Nor can he understand the words, “Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord” (Jeremiah 23:24). Nor does he see that, according to the Christians’ teaching, “in him we all live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28), as Paul too taught in his speech to the Athenians.

So even if the God of the universe, by his own power, comes down with Jesus into the life of men, and even if the Word who was “in the beginning with God,” and who is himself “God” (John 1:1–2), comes to us, he is not displaced, nor does he leave his own seat, as though one place were empty of him and another, which did not have him before, were full. The power and divinity of God comes to dwell through whom he wills and in whom it finds room, while he neither changes place nor leaves his own place empty and fills another.

For even if we should say that he leaves one and fills another, we shall not be declaring this about place. Rather, we shall say that the soul of the wicked man, dissipated in vice, is forsaken by God, while we shall declare that the soul of one who wishes to live according to virtue, or is making progress, or already lives according to it, is filled with the divine Spirit or shares in it.

There is no need, then, for the descent of Christ, or for God’s turning toward men, that a greater seat be left behind and the things here be changed, as Celsus thinks when he says: “For if you were to change even one thing here, the very least, everything would be overturned and gone.” But if we must speak of anyone being changed by the presence of God’s power and the coming of the Word to men, we shall not hesitate to say that whoever has received the coming of the Word of God into his own soul is changed from wicked to good, from licentious to self-controlled, and from superstitious to reverent.

title: God does not show off like the newly rich
english: If you want us to answer even the most ridiculous of Celsus’s remarks, listen to what he says: “But then, would God, being unknown among men and thinking himself the worse off for it, wish to become known and to put to the test both those who believe and those who do not, like the newly rich among men who love to show off? They charge God with a great and altogether mortal love of honour.”

We say, then, that God, being unknown to wicked men, would wish to be known, not because he thinks himself the worse off, but because the knowledge of him frees the one who knows him from misery. Nor is it from a wish to test those who believe or those who do not that he either comes himself, by an ineffable and divine power, to dwell in certain people, or sends his Christ. He does it so that those who believe and grasp his divinity may be freed from all misery, while those who do not believe may no longer have room even for the plea that they did not believe because they had not heard and been taught.

What argument, then, shows that it follows from our teaching that God, as we conceive him, is like the newly rich among men who love to show off? For God does not show off before us out of a wish that we should understand and perceive his surpassing greatness. Rather, wishing to plant in us the blessedness that arises in our souls from our knowing him, he works through Christ and through the Word’s continual coming among us, so that we may take up our kinship with him. So the Christian teaching charges God with no mortal love of honour.

title: God has always cared for human life
english: I do not know how, after talking idle nonsense about the points we have set out, he later sets out the view that it is not because he needs to be known for his own sake, but for the sake of our salvation, that God wishes to give us knowledge of himself, so that those who accept it may become good and be saved, while those who do not accept it may be shown to be wicked and be punished. And having set this out, he raises a further difficulty, saying: “So it is only now, after so long an age, that God has remembered to set human life right, while before he did not care?”

To this too we shall say that there was never a time when God did not wish to set human life right. He has always cared for it, giving starting points for virtue so that the rational creature might be set right. For in every generation the wisdom of God, passing into souls that it finds holy, makes them friends of God and prophets (Wisdom of Solomon 7:27). And in the sacred books one could find those who in each generation were holy and able to receive the divine Spirit, and how they converted the people of their own day, as far as their power allowed.

title: The nations allotted to angels, then given to Christ
english: Nor is it any wonder that in certain generations there have been prophets who, through their more strenuous and vigorous lives, surpassed other prophets in receiving the divine, some of whom lived in their own time and others earlier or later. In the same way it is no wonder that there was also a certain time when something exceptional came to dwell among the human race, something that surpassed those who came before it, or even those after it. But the account of these matters holds something more mystical and deeper, which cannot easily reach the ears of the common crowd.

And to make these things clear, and to answer what is said about Christ’s coming, “So it is only now, after so long an age, that God has remembered to set the human race right, while before he did not care?”, we must touch on the doctrine of the portions and make clear why “when the Most High divided the nations, as he scattered the sons of Adam, he set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God; and his people Jacob became the Lord’s portion, Israel the measured lot of his inheritance” (Deuteronomy 32:8–9). We shall need to state the reason for being born into each territory under the one to whom that territory was allotted, and how it was with good reason that “his people Jacob became the Lord’s portion, Israel the measured lot of his inheritance” (Deuteronomy 32:9); and why formerly “the Lord’s portion was his people Jacob, Israel the measured lot of his inheritance” (Deuteronomy 32:9), whereas of later times the Father says to the Saviour: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession” (Psalm 2:8). For there are certain connections and sequences, unspeakable and beyond telling, in the varied ordering of human souls.

title: Christ, the reformer of the whole world
english: So, whether Celsus likes it or not, after many prophets who had set right the affairs of that Israel, Christ came as the one who sets right the whole world. He did not need, as under the former dispensation, to use whips and chains and tortures against men; for his teaching was enough, when “the sower went out to sow” (Matthew 13:3), so that he might sow the word everywhere (Mark 4:14).

If a time is to come that will bound the world, a limit made necessary by its having had a beginning, and if an end is to come upon the world, and after the end a just judgement upon all, then the one who pursues these questions as a philosopher will need to establish the points of our teaching with proofs of every kind, both from the divine writings and from the logical sequence of the arguments. But the ordinary, simpler person, who cannot follow the most intricate insights of the wisdom of God, once he has entrusted himself to God and to the Saviour of our race, will need to be content with “He himself said it” of this Saviour rather than of anyone else at all.

title: Threats of punishment and promises of the kingdom
english: After this, as is his habit, Celsus again establishes and proves nothing, but, as though we talked about God without holiness or reverence, he says: “That they talk on about God in this way without holiness or reverence is quite plain.” He thinks that we do these things to astonish the uneducated, and not because we speak the truth about punishments that are necessary for those who have sinned. That is why he likens us to those who, in the Bacchic mysteries, bring on the phantoms and terrors beforehand.

Now as to the Bacchic mysteries, whether there is any convincing account of them or none at all, let the Greeks speak, and let Celsus and his fellow revellers listen. We, for our part, make our defence for our own teaching, saying that our aim is to set the human race right. We do this either through the threats of punishment, which we are persuaded are necessary for the universe, and perhaps not without use even to those who will suffer them, or through the promises made to those who have lived well, which hold out the blessed life in the kingdom of God for those worthy to have him reign over them.

title: Moses is older than the theorists of world cycles
english: Next, wishing to show that we say nothing remarkable or new about a flood or a conflagration, but that we misheard what Greeks or barbarians say about these things and then believed our own Scriptures about them, he says this: “This too occurred to them because they misheard those others: that in long cycles of time, and with the returns and conjunctions of the stars, conflagrations and floods take place, and that after the last flood, in the time of Deucalion, the cycle, in keeping with the alternation of the universe, requires a conflagration. This made them say, in their mistaken opinion, that God will come down like a torturer bearing fire.”

To this too we shall reply: I do not know how Celsus, who has read so much and has shown that he knows many histories, failed to take note of the antiquity of Moses. Certain Greek writers record that Moses lived in the times of Inachus, father of Phoroneus, and he is admitted to be very ancient by the Egyptians, and also by those who have written on the history of Phoenicia. Anyone who wishes may read the two books of Flavius Josephus on the antiquity of the Jews (Josephus, Against Apion), to learn how Moses was older than those who said that floods and conflagrations happen in the world over long periods of time. Celsus says that Jews and Christians misheard these men and, not understanding what they said about the conflagration, said that God will come down like a torturer bearing fire.

title: What it means that God comes down
english: Whether there are cycles, and floods or conflagrations by cycles, or not, and whether our teaching also knows of these things, in many passages and especially where Solomon says, “What is it that has been? The very thing that shall be. And what is it that has been done? The very thing that shall be done” (Ecclesiastes 1:9), and what follows, it is not the present occasion to say. It is enough only to note that Moses and some of the prophets, who were men of the greatest antiquity, did not take from others what they say about the conflagration of the world. Rather, if we must attend to the dates and say so, it was others who misheard them and, not grasping exactly what they said, made up the idea that in each cycle the very same things recur, indistinguishable down to their individual qualities and their accidents.

We, however, ascribe neither the flood nor the conflagration to cycles and periods of the stars. We say that their cause is wickedness, spreading ever further and purged by a flood or a conflagration. And if the prophetic words speak of God coming down, the God who said, “Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord” (Jeremiah 23:24), we take it figuratively. For God comes down from his own greatness and height when he orders the affairs of men, and above all of the wicked. And just as ordinary usage says that teachers come down to little children, and that the wise, or those making progress, come down to young people who have just turned to philosophy, not meaning that they come down bodily, so wherever in the divine Scriptures God is said to come down, it is understood in the same way as this ordinary use of the word; and so too with going up.

title: Our God is a consuming fire
english: Since Celsus mocks us, saying that we claim God comes down like a torturer bearing fire, and so forces us to examine deeper doctrines out of season, we shall say a little, just enough to give our hearers a taste of a defence that overturns Celsus’s mockery of us, and then turn to what follows. The divine word says that our God is “a consuming fire” (Deuteronomy 4:24; Hebrews 12:29), and that “rivers of fire flow before him” (Daniel 7:10), and also that he himself comes in “like a refiner’s fire and like fullers’ herb,” to refine his own people (Malachi 3:2–3).

So when he is said to be “a consuming fire” (Deuteronomy 4:24), we ask what it is fitting for God to consume. And we say that God, as fire, consumes wickedness and the deeds that spring from it, which are figuratively called “wood” and “hay” and “straw.” For the wicked man is said to “build” “wood” and “hay” and “straw” upon the rational foundation already laid (1 Corinthians 3:10–12). Now if anyone can show that the writer meant these words otherwise, and can present the wicked man as building “wood” or “hay” or “straw” in a bodily sense, then clearly the fire too will be understood as material and perceptible. But if the works of the wicked man are plainly spoken of figuratively when they are called “wood” or “hay” or “straw,” how is it not obvious at once what kind of fire is meant, by which such “wood” is to be consumed? For he says: “The fire itself will test what sort of work each one has done. If anyone’s work that he has built upon it remains, he will receive a reward; if anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss” (1 Corinthians 3:13–15). And what work burned up could be meant in these words, if not everything done out of wickedness?

Our God, then, is “a consuming fire” (Deuteronomy 4:24) in the sense we have given, and so he “comes in like a refiner’s fire” (Malachi 3:2), to refine the rational nature, which is filled with the lead of wickedness and with the other impure materials that have debased the golden nature of the soul, if I may call it so, or its silver nature. So too “rivers of fire” are said to be “before” God (Daniel 7:10), who will utterly do away with the wickedness mixed through the whole soul. But this is enough in reply to the words: “This made them say, in their mistaken opinion, that God will come down like a torturer bearing fire.”

title: God comes down without changing
english: Let us look also at what Celsus says next, with a grand announcement, in this way: “Further,” he says, “let us take up the argument again from the beginning with more proofs. I say nothing new, only what has long been settled. God is good and beautiful and happy, and is in what is most beautiful and best. If, then, he comes down to men, he must undergo change: a change from good to bad, from beautiful to shameful, from happiness to misery, and from what is best to what is most wicked. Who would choose such a change? Besides, it is the nature of what is mortal to be altered and remoulded, but of what is immortal to remain the same and unchanging. So God would not accept this change either.”

To this, it seems to me, the needful answer is given by explaining what the Scriptures say about the descent of God to human affairs. For this he needs no change, as Celsus thinks we say, nor any turning from good to bad, or from beautiful to shameful, or from happiness to misery, or from what is best to what is most wicked. For, remaining unchangeable in his essence, he comes down to human affairs by his providence and his ordering of things.

We, then, show that the divine writings also speak of God as unchangeable, both in the words “But you are the same” (Psalm 102:27) and in “I have not changed” (Malachi 3:6). But the gods of Epicurus, being made up of atoms and, so far as their structure goes, liable to dissolve, are busy shaking off the atoms that would destroy them. And the god of the Stoics too, since he is a body, at one time has the whole of substance as his ruling part, when the conflagration takes place, and at another comes to be in a part of it, when the world is set in order. For these men have not been able to bring out clearly the natural conception of God as in every way incorruptible, simple, uncompounded and indivisible.

title: The Word humbled himself but did not change
english: What came down to men existed “in the form of God” (Philippians 2:6), and out of love for mankind “emptied himself” (Philippians 2:7), so that he could be received by men. Surely no change from good to bad took place in him, for “he committed no sin” (1 Peter 2:22); nor from beautiful to shameful, for he “knew no sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21). Nor did he pass from happiness to misery: he “humbled himself” (Philippians 2:8), yet he was no less blessed, even while he humbled himself for the good of our race. Nor did any change take place in him from what is best to what is most wicked; for how can kindness and love for mankind be most wicked?

Or is it time to say that the physician too, who looks on dreadful sights and handles loathsome things in order to heal the sick, passes from good to bad, or from beautiful to shameful, or from happiness to misery? And yet the physician who looks on dreadful sights and handles loathsome things does not wholly escape the risk of falling into the same ills himself. But he who heals “the wounds” of our souls through the Word of God that was in him could himself admit no evil at all.

But if Celsus thinks that the immortal God the Word, by taking up a mortal body and a human soul, is altered and remoulded, let him learn that “the Word” (John 1:14), remaining Word in essence, suffers none of the things that the body or the soul suffers. Rather, coming down at times to one who cannot look upon the flashing radiance and brightness of his Godhead, he becomes as it were “flesh” (John 1:14), and is spoken in a bodily way, until the one who has received him in this form is lifted up little by little by the Word and becomes able to behold even his primary form, if I may call it that.

title: The Word shows different forms to different hearers
english: For there are, as it were, different forms of the Word, as the Word appears to each of those who are being led into knowledge, in proportion to the state of each: the one who is just beginning, or who has made a little progress or more, or is already drawing near to virtue, or has even come to live in virtue.

Hence, not in the way Celsus and those like him would have it, our God “was transfigured” and, going up “onto the high mountain” (Matthew 17:1-2; Mark 9:2), showed another form of himself, far better than the one seen by those who stayed below and could not follow him to the height. For those below did not have eyes able to see the transfiguration of the Word into what is glorious and more divine. They could barely receive him as he was, so that those who could not see his better form might say of him: “We saw him, and he had no form or beauty; but his form was without honour, falling short of the sons of men” (Isaiah 53:2-3).

Let this be said in answer to the supposition of Celsus, who did not understand the changes or transformations of Jesus that are told in the manner of historical narrative, nor what is mortal or immortal in him.

title: A worthier story than the myth of Dionysus
english: Will not these things, especially when they are understood in the right way, appear far more dignified than Dionysus being deceived by the Titans, falling from the throne of Zeus, being torn to pieces by them, and afterwards being put together again and, as it were, coming back to life and going up to heaven? Or are the Greeks allowed to refer such tales to the doctrine of the soul and to interpret them figuratively, while the door is shut on us to a coherent explanation, one that everywhere agrees and harmonises with the Scriptures that come from the divine Spirit, who has dwelt in pure souls?

Celsus, then, has by no means seen the purpose of our writings, and so it is his own interpretation, not that of the Scriptures, that he attacks. Had he considered what follows for a soul that is to live in eternal life, and what one ought to think about its essence and its origins, he would not have mocked in this way the immortal one coming into a mortal body, not according to Plato’s transmigration of souls but according to some other, loftier view.

He would also have seen one exceptional descent, made out of great love for mankind, to bring back what the divine Scripture has called, in a hidden sense, “the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24), which had come down from the mountains; and to these the shepherd in certain parables is said to have come down, leaving on the mountains those that had not gone astray (Matthew 18:12; Luke 15:4).

title: The Word becomes food fitted to each
english: By lingering over things he has not understood, Celsus makes us repeat ourselves, since we do not wish even to seem to have left any of his statements unexamined. He says next: “Either God really changes, as these people say, into a mortal body, and it has already been said that he cannot; or he himself does not change, but makes those who see him think he has, and leads them astray and lies. But deceit and falsehood are evils in every other case; one might use them only as a kind of medicine, either toward friends who are sick or mad, to heal them, or toward enemies, when one is taking care to escape danger. But no one who is sick or mad is a friend of God, nor does God fear anyone, that he should lead him astray to escape danger.”

To this one may answer partly concerning the nature of the divine Word, who is God, and partly concerning the soul of Jesus. Concerning the nature of the Word: just as the quality of foods is changed into milk in the nurse to suit the nature of the infant, or is prepared by the physician to meet the sick man’s need for health, or is made ready accordingly for the stronger man, since he is more able to take it; so God changes the power of the Word, whose nature is to nourish the human soul, for each person according to his worth. To one, as Scripture has named it, he becomes “the pure milk of the word” (1 Peter 2:2); to another, who is weaker, something like vegetables (Romans 14:2); to another, who is mature, he is given as “solid food” (Hebrews 5:14). And surely the Word does not belie his own nature when he becomes nourishment for each, as each is able to receive him; he neither leads astray nor lies.

But if someone takes the change to refer to the soul of Jesus, when it came into a body, we shall ask what he means by “change”. If he means change of essence, that is not granted, either for that soul or for any other rational soul. But if he means that, being mingled with the body, it suffers something from the body and from the place into which it has come, what absurdity follows for the teaching that, out of great love for mankind, brings a Saviour down to the human race? For none of those who earlier professed to heal could do as much as this soul showed by what it did, even coming down willingly, for the sake of our race, into the ills that are the lot of men.

Knowing this, the divine word says much in many places of the Scriptures. For the present it is enough to set out one passage of Paul, which runs thus: “Have this mind among you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count being equal with God a prize to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave; and being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him and granted him a name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:5-9).

title: No deceit in the Saviour’s coming
english: Let others, then, grant Celsus that he does not change, but makes those who see him think he has changed. We, however, who are convinced that in the coming of Jesus among men there was no semblance but truth and plain reality, are not open to Celsus’s charge.

Even so, we will make this answer: Do you not say, Celsus, that it is sometimes permitted to use deceit and lying as a kind of medicine? What is absurd, then, in something of this kind having taken place, if something of this kind was going to bring salvation? For some words, when spoken falsely rather than truthfully, turn certain characters back, as do some words that physicians at times speak to the sick. But let this be our defence on behalf of others.

For it is not absurd that he who heals friends who are sick should heal the human race, which is dear to him, by such means as one would not use by preference, but because circumstances demand it. And the human race, being mad, had to be cured by methods that the Word saw were useful for the mad, so that they might come to their senses.

He says, too, that one does such things toward enemies, “when one is taking care to escape danger”. But God does not fear anyone, so as to escape danger by leading astray those who plot against him. It is wholly superfluous and unreasonable to answer what no one says about our Saviour.

As for the words “But no one who is sick or mad is a friend of God”, an answer has already been given in our defence on behalf of others. For whoever makes that defence says that such a dispensation takes place not for those who are already friends and are sick or mad, but for those who, through sickness of soul and the derangement of their natural reasoning, are still enemies (Romans 5:10), so that they may become friends of God. For it is plainly said that Jesus took all things upon himself for sinners (Romans 5:8), that he might “set them free” from sin (Hebrews 2:15) and make them “righteous” (Romans 5:19).

title: Why a cleansing coming is not absurd
english: Next, he brings on stage, on one side, Jews who explain the reason for the coming of Christ, a coming that in their view still lies in the future, and on the other side, Christians who speak of the coming of the Son of God into human life as something that has already taken place. Come, then, let us look into these points too, as briefly as we can.

The Jews in his book say that human life, filled with every kind of wickedness, needs one sent down from God, so that the unjust may be punished and all things purified, as in the first flood (compare Genesis 6:11–13; Genesis 7:21–23). And since the Christians too are said to add other things to these, it is plain that he says these things are said by them as well.

And what is absurd in this, that when wickedness has overflowed, one will come who will cleanse the world and deal with each according to what each deserves? For it does not befit God to leave the spread of wickedness unchecked and not to renew the order of things. The Greeks, too, know of the earth being cleansed at set periods by flood or by fire, as Plato also says somewhere: “Whenever the gods cleanse the earth with waters and flood it, those in the mountains…” (Plato, Timaeus 22d), and the rest.

We must ask, then: if the Greeks say these things, is what they proclaim solemn and worth a hearing, but if we too argue for some of these very things that the Greeks praise, are these doctrines no longer good? And yet those who are concerned with setting out clearly and exactly all that has been written will try to show not only the antiquity of those who wrote these things, but also the dignity of what they said and its consistency.

title: The tower, Sodom and the cleansing fire
english: I do not know how he thinks that the overthrow of the tower also took place in the same way as the flood that cleansed the earth, as the teaching of Jews and Christians would have it. For even granting that the story of the tower set down in Genesis (Genesis 11:1–9) speaks in no riddles but, as Celsus thinks, is plain, not even so does it appear that this happened to cleanse the earth; unless, perhaps, he thinks that what is called the “confusion” of tongues (Genesis 11:9) was a cleansing of the earth. Whoever is able will give an account of this at a more suitable time, when the task in hand is to set out both what sense the story in that passage has and what its higher meaning is.

He thinks that Moses, who recorded the events of the tower and the confusion of languages, corrupted the stories told about the sons of Aloeus and so recorded such things about the tower. To this it must be said that I do not think anyone told the stories of the sons of Aloeus before Homer, whereas I am persuaded that Moses recorded the events of the tower, which are much older than Homer and even than the invention of Greek letters. Who, then, is more likely to be corrupting whose stories? Do those who tell of the sons of Aloeus corrupt the events of the tower, or does the man who wrote of the tower and the confusion of languages corrupt the stories of the Aloadae? But to impartial hearers Moses plainly appears to be older than Homer.

Moses also tells in Genesis of Sodom and Gomorrah, how they were wiped out by fire because of their sin (Genesis 19:24–25). Celsus compares this with the story of Phaethon, doing everything in keeping with his one mistake, his failure to take account of the antiquity of Moses. For those who tell of Phaethon seem to be younger even than Homer, and Homer is much younger than Moses.

We do not deny, then, the cleansing fire and the destruction of the world for the removal of wickedness and the renewal of the universe, and we say that we have learned this from the prophets, out of the sacred books. Yet once the prophets, who say many things about the future, are shown, as we said above, to have spoken the truth about many things that are past, and to give proof that the divine Spirit was in them, it is plain that we must believe them about the things to come as well, or rather believe the divine Spirit in them.

title: The fall of Jerusalem and the new call
english: According to Celsus, the Christians add some further points to what the Jews say, and claim that the Son of God has already been sent because of the sins of the Jews, and that the Jews, by punishing Jesus and giving him gall to drink (Matthew 27:34), drew down wrath from God upon themselves.

Let anyone who wishes prove this statement false, if the whole Jewish nation was not overthrown before even one full generation had passed since Jesus suffered these things at their hands. For it was, I think, forty-two years from the time they crucified Jesus to the destruction of Jerusalem. And never, since there have been Jews, has it been recorded that they were shut out for so long a time from their venerable rites and worship, overpowered by those stronger than they. But even if at times they seemed to be abandoned because of their sins, they were none the less visited, and they returned and recovered what was their own, performing their customary rites without hindrance. So one of the facts that show Jesus to have been something divine and holy is this: that on his account so many and such great calamities have now befallen the Jews for a long time.

We shall say with confidence that they will not even be restored. For they committed the most unholy crime of all, when they plotted against the Saviour of the human race in the very city where they used to perform for God the customary rites that were symbols of great mysteries. It was necessary, then, that the city where Jesus suffered these things should be utterly destroyed, that the Jewish nation should be overthrown, and that God’s call to blessedness should pass to others, I mean the Christians. To them has come the teaching of sincere and pure devotion to God, and they have received new laws suited to the order of life established everywhere, since the laws given earlier, as to one nation ruled by kings of its own race and customs, could not all be carried out now.

title: Celsus likens Jews and Christians to worms
english: After this, laughing in his usual way, he has compared the race of Jews and Christians, all of them, to a cluster of bats, or to ants coming out of a nest, or to frogs holding council around a marsh, or to worms holding an assembly in a corner of the mire and quarrelling with one another over which of them are the greater sinners, and saying: “God reveals and announces everything to us beforehand; he has left the whole world and the movement of the heavens, he has disregarded this vast earth, and he lives as a fellow citizen with us alone; to us alone he sends his heralds, and he never stops sending and seeking how we may be with him for ever.”

And in his own fiction he makes us like worms who say: “There is God, and after him come we, made by him and wholly like God (compare Genesis 1:26–28); and all things have been put under us, earth and water and air and stars; all things exist for our sake, and have been appointed to serve us.” And the worms in his account, meaning us, of course, say: “Now, since some among us do wrong, God will come or will send his Son to burn up the unjust, so that the rest of us may have eternal life with him.” And to all this he adds that such claims are more tolerable coming from worms and frogs than from Jews and Christians quarrelling with one another.

title: Littleness is not measured by the body
english: In reply to this we ask those who accept what has been said against us in this way, and we say: Do you suppose that all human beings are a cluster of bats, or ants, or frogs, or worms, because of God’s surpassing greatness? Or do you leave the rest of humankind out of the picture set before us, and because of their reason and their established laws keep them as human beings, while you belittle Christians and Jews because of their doctrines, which do not please you, and so have compared them to these animals?

Whichever answer you give to our question, we shall reply by trying to show that such things have not been rightly said, whether of all human beings or of us. Suppose, first, you say that all human beings, in relation to God, are compared with these mean animals, since their littleness can in no way be compared with God’s surpassing greatness. What littleness do you mean? Answer me, you there.

If you mean the littleness of their bodies, hear this: when truth is the judge, what surpasses and what falls short is not decided by the body. For on that reckoning griffins and elephants will be better than us human beings, since they are larger and stronger and longer-lived than we are. Yet no one of sound mind would say that these irrational creatures are better than rational beings because of their bodies (for reason raises the rational being far above all irrational ones). Nor would he say that the virtuous and blessed beings are better because of their bodies, whether these are, as you say, the good demons, or, as we are accustomed to call them, the angels of God, or whatever natures there may be that surpass human beings; he would say they are better because the reason in them has been brought to perfection and formed in every virtue.

title: No rational soul is a worm
english: But suppose you scorn man’s littleness not because of the body but because of the soul, on the ground that it is inferior to the other rational beings, and especially to the virtuous ones, and inferior for this reason, that wickedness is in it. Why, then, are the bad among Christians and those among Jews who live evil lives any more a cluster of bats, or ants, or worms, or frogs, than the wicked among the other nations? On this reckoning anyone at all, and above all one given over to unrestrained wickedness, is a bat and a worm and a frog and an ant compared with the rest of humankind.

So even if a man is Demosthenes the orator, with wickedness like his and the deeds he did out of wickedness, or Antiphon, who is also reckoned an orator and who denied providence in the books entitled On Truth, a title like that of Celsus, none the less these men are worms rolling about in a corner of the mire of folly and ignorance.

And yet no rational being of any kind whatever could reasonably be compared to a worm, since it has starting points for virtue. For these first sketches of virtue do not allow those who have virtue in potential, and who cannot wholly lose its seeds, to be compared to a worm. It appears, then, that human beings in general could not be worms in relation to God, for reason, which takes its beginning from the Word who comes from God, does not allow the rational living being to be thought wholly alien to God. Nor could the bad among Christians and Jews, who in truth are neither Christians nor Jews, be compared to worms rolling about in a corner of the mire any more than the other bad.

And if the nature of reason does not allow us to accept even this, then plainly we shall not insult human nature, which was made for virtue, even if it sins through ignorance, nor shall we liken it to such animals.

title: Who the real worms are
english: But if, because of the doctrines of Christians and Jews that displease Celsus (doctrines he seems not to understand at all), these people are worms and ants while the rest of mankind are not, come, let us examine the doctrines of Christians and Jews that are plain to everyone at first sight, and compare them with those of the rest of mankind. Let us see whether it will not become clear, to anyone who once grants that some human beings are worms and ants, who the worms and ants and frogs really are. They are those who have fallen away from a sound conception of God and, under a semblance of piety, worship irrational animals or images, or even the things that have been made (Romans 1:23, 25), when they ought to marvel at the Maker from the beauty of what he has made (Wisdom of Solomon 13:3–5) and to worship him. Human beings, on the other hand, and anything more honourable than human beings, are those who, following reason, have been able to rise above stones and wood, and even above silver and gold, the matter that is reckoned most precious. They have risen also from the beautiful things in the world to the one who made the universe and have entrusted themselves to him. They send up their prayers to him as the only one who is able to suffice for all that exists, to watch over the thoughts of all, and to hear the prayer of all. They do everything as in the sight of one who sees all that is done, and as before one who hears all that is said they take care to say nothing that, as it reaches God, would not please him.

Unless, of course, such great piety, which is overcome neither by sufferings nor by the danger of death nor by persuasive arguments, does nothing to keep those who have taken it up from being compared any longer to worms, even if they were so compared before they came to such piety! Take those who overcome the fiercest of appetites, the appetite for sexual pleasure, which has made the hearts of many soft as wax. They overcome it for this reason: they have been persuaded that they cannot otherwise be made God’s own unless they also rise to him through self-control. Do these seem to us to be brothers of worms, kin of ants, and like frogs? And what of the splendour of justice, which preserves fellowship, fairness, humanity and kindness toward one’s neighbour and fellow human being? Does it do nothing to keep such a person from being a bat?

But those who wallow in licentiousness, as most people do, and those who go to common prostitutes as a matter of indifference and even teach that this is not at all contrary to what is fitting, are they not worms in the mire? Above all when they are compared with those who have been taught not to take “the members of Christ” and the body in which the Word dwells and make them “members of a prostitute” (1 Corinthians 6:15)? These have learned already that the “body” of a rational being, dedicated to the God of the universe, “is a temple” of the God whom they worship (1 Corinthians 6:19), and that it becomes such through a pure conception of the Creator. Guarding against destroying “the temple of God” (1 Corinthians 3:17) through unlawful intercourse, they practise self-control as piety toward God.

title: Those who truly bear the name of Christian
english: And I do not yet speak of the other evils found among human beings, from which not even those who are reputed to be philosophers are readily free (for in philosophy too there are many counterfeits). Nor do I yet say that such evils abound among those who are neither Jews nor Christians, while among Christians they either do not exist at all, if you examine strictly who the Christian is, or, if they should be found, are certainly not found among those who meet together, come to the common prayers, and are not shut out from them; unless perhaps, on rare occasions, someone of that sort is found escaping notice among the many.

So we are not worms holding assembly, we who take our stand against the Jews on the basis of the writings they believe to be sacred, and who show that the one who was prophesied has come; that they have been forsaken because of their very great sins; and that we who have received the word have the best hopes with God, both from our faith in him and from a life that is able to make us, pure from all wickedness and vice, his own.

It is not, then, simply anyone who proclaims himself a Jew or a Christian who could say that God made the whole world and the motion of the heavens chiefly for us. But if someone is, as Jesus taught, pure “in heart” (Matthew 5:8), meek (Matthew 5:5), a peacemaker (Matthew 5:9), and one who readily endures dangers for the sake of piety (Matthew 5:10–11), such a person might with good reason have confidence in God; and, understanding the meaning of the prophecies as well, he might also say that God has shown all these things beforehand and announced them to us who believe.

title: God loves all that he has made
english: Celsus has represented those he considers worms, the Christians, as saying that “God has left the motion of the heavens and disregarded the vast earth, and makes his home among us alone, sends his envoys to us, and never ceases sending and seeking how we may be with him forever.” To this we must reply that he attributes to us things that we do not say. For we read and know that God loves all things that exist and loathes none of the things he has made, for he would not have fashioned anything if he hated it (Wisdom of Solomon 11:24). We have also read: “You spare all things, for they are yours, O Lover of souls. For your imperishable Spirit is in all things. Therefore you correct little by little those who fall away, and you admonish them by reminding them of the things in which they sin” (Wisdom of Solomon 11:26–12:2).

How could we say that God has left the motion of the heavens and the whole world, and disregarded the vast earth, to make his home among us alone? We have found that in our prayers we must speak as people convinced that “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Psalm 33:5), and that “the mercy of the Lord is upon all flesh” (Sirach 18:13); and that God, being good, “makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust” (Matthew 5:45). He urges us to do the like, so that we may become his sons (Matthew 5:44–45), and teaches us to extend our good deeds to all people as far as we can. For he himself is called “the Saviour of all people, especially of believers” (1 Timothy 4:10), and his Christ is called “the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the whole world” (1 John 2:2).

Perhaps some of the Jews might say, not the things Celsus has recorded, but certain other naive things; but certainly not Christians, who have been taught that “God shows his own love for us in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). And yet “one will scarcely die for a righteous man; though for a good man someone might perhaps even dare to die” (Romans 5:7). But as it is, Jesus is proclaimed to have come for sinners everywhere, so that they may leave sin behind and entrust themselves to God; and by a usage long established in these writings he is also called the Christ of God.

title: How “God, then we” can be rightly understood
english: Perhaps Celsus misheard some people saying, “There is God, and after him come we,” we whom he has called worms. He acts like those who find fault with a whole school of philosophy because of things said by some rash youth who has attended a philosopher’s lectures for three days and looks down on everyone else as inferior and ignorant of philosophy. For we know that there are many beings more honourable than man. We have read that “God stood in the assembly of gods” (Psalm 82:1), gods who are not those worshipped by the rest of mankind (for “all the gods of the nations are demons,” Psalm 96:5); and we have read that “God,” standing “in the assembly of gods, judges gods in their midst” (Psalm 82:1). We know too that “although there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, as indeed there are many gods and many lords, yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we are for him, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him” (1 Corinthians 8:5–6).

We know also that the angels are so far above human beings that human beings, once made perfect, become equal to angels; for “in the resurrection of the dead” the righteous “neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of heaven” (Matthew 22:30; compare Mark 12:25), and they become “equal to angels” (Luke 20:36). We know that in the ordering of the universe there are some who are called thrones, others dominions, others authorities and others rulers (Colossians 1:16). And we see that we human beings, though we fall far short of these, have hope that by living well and doing everything in accordance with reason we shall rise to a likeness with all of them. And lastly, since “it has not yet been revealed what we shall be, we know that when he is revealed we shall be like God and shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

But if someone were to say what is said by some, whether by those who understand or by those who do not understand but have misheard sound teaching, that “there is God, and after him come we,” I would interpret even this, taking “we” to mean rational beings, and still more the virtuous among rational beings. For in our view the same virtue belongs to all the blessed, so that the virtue of a human being and of God is also the same. That is why we are taught to become “perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5:48). So no one who is noble and good is a worm swimming in the mire, no one who is pious is an ant, no one who is righteous is a frog, and no one whose soul is lit by the bright light of truth could reasonably be compared to a bat.

title: Made in the image, not yet in the likeness
english: It seems to me that Celsus has also misheard the words “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26), and on that basis has made the worms say, “Since we were made by God, we are in every way like him.” Yet if he had known the difference between man’s having been made “according to the image” of God and his being made “according to the likeness,” and that it is written that God said, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26), but that God made man “according to the image” of God (Genesis 1:27), and not yet also “according to the likeness,” he would not have made us say that we are in every way like God.

Nor do we say that the stars too have been made subject to us. For the resurrection of the righteous, as it is spoken of and as the wise understand it, is compared to the sun and moon and stars by him who says: “There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory. So also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15:41–42); and Daniel too prophesied of these things long ago (Daniel 12:3).

He claims that we say, “All things have been appointed to serve us.” Perhaps he has not heard the intelligent among us saying such things; perhaps, too, he does not understand in what sense it has been said that the greater among us is the servant of all (Matthew 23:11; Mark 10:44). And when Greeks say, “Then sun and night serve mortals” (Euripides, Phoenician Women 546), they praise the saying and expound it; but when such a thing is either not said among us or said in another sense, Celsus slanders us even on these grounds.

In Celsus’s book we, who in his account are worms, were saying that “since some among us go wrong, God will come to us, or will send his own Son, to burn up the unrighteous, so that the rest of us frogs may have eternal life with him.” And see how this solemn philosopher, like a buffoon, has turned to mockery, laughter and ridicule the divine proclamation about judgment and about the punishment “against the unrighteous” and the reward for the righteous. To all this he adds that these things “are more bearable when worms and frogs say them than when Jews and Christians, quarrelling with one another, proclaim them.”

But we will not imitate him, nor will we say the like about the philosophers who profess to know the nature of the universe, and who debate with one another about how the universe was put together, how heaven and earth and all that is in them came to be, and whether souls, being unbegotten and not created by God, are set in order by him and pass from body to body, or, being sown together with bodies, outlast them or do not outlast them. For someone could mock and revile these things too, instead of speaking of them with respect and approving the purpose of those who have devoted themselves to the search for truth, and say that these men are worms in a corner of the mire of human life, who do not take their own measure and for that reason pronounce on such great matters as though they had grasped them; and that they speak insistently, as men who have beheld them, about things that cannot be beheld without the inspiration of a higher and more divine power. “For no one among men knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that is in him; so also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2:11).

But we are not mad, and we do not compare so great an understanding in men (I use “understanding” in its looser sense), one that has busied itself not with the concerns of the many but with the search for truth, to the movements of worms or of any other such creatures. Rather, as lovers of truth, we bear witness concerning some of the Greek philosophers that they came to know God, since “God made it plain to them” (Romans 1:19), even if “they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their reasonings” (Romans 1:21), and “claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man and of birds and four-footed beasts and creeping things” (Romans 1:22–23).

title: The commonwealth of the Hebrews
english: After this, wishing to establish that Jews and Christians differ in no way from the creatures he named earlier, he says that “the Jews were runaways from Egypt, who never did anything worth mentioning, and were never of any account or number.” Now, that they were not runaways, nor Egyptians, but Hebrews who lived as sojourners in Egypt, we have already said above. But if he thinks it is proved that they were “of no account or number” from the fact that their history is scarcely to be found among the Greeks, we will say that if anyone looks closely at their commonwealth from its beginning and at the ordering of their laws, he would find that they were men who showed on earth a shadow of the heavenly life.

Among them nothing else was held to be God but the One who is over all, and none of those who make images had a place among their citizens. For there was neither painter nor sculptor in their commonwealth, since the law banished all such people from it, so that there might be no occasion for the making of statues, which lures the foolish among men and drags the eyes of the soul down from God to earth. So they had a law such as this: “Do not act lawlessly and make for yourselves a carved likeness, any image, a likeness of male or female, a likeness of any beast of those that are on the earth, a likeness of any winged bird that flies under heaven, a likeness of any creeping thing that creeps on the earth, a likeness of any fish, all that are in the waters beneath the earth” (Deuteronomy 4:16–18). Indeed, the law wished them to keep company with the truth about each thing and not to fashion other things contrary to the truth, counterfeiting what is truly male or really female, or the nature of beasts, or the kind of birds, of creeping things, or of fish.

Solemn and lofty, too, is their precept: “Do not, when you look up to heaven and see the sun and the moon and the stars, all the array of heaven, be led astray and bow down to them and serve them” (Deuteronomy 4:19). And what a commonwealth it was, that of a whole nation in which it was not even possible for an effeminate man to be seen! Wonderful, too, is the fact that the courtesans, who inflame the young, were removed from their commonwealth (Deuteronomy 23:17). They had courts made up of the most just men, men who had given proof of a sound life over a long time, to whom judgments were entrusted; and these, because of their pure character and what in them was more than human, were called gods, by an ancestral custom of the Jews. One could see a whole nation practising philosophy; and, to give leisure for hearing the divine laws, there were the so-called sabbaths and their other [ordinances], those of priests and of sacrifices, which contain countless symbols made clear to those who love learning.

title: From Israel’s law to the worship Jesus brought
english: But since nothing in human nature is secure, that commonwealth too had to decay little by little and fall away from its way of life. And providence, having remodelled what was solemn in the teaching of the Jews where it needed remodelling, so as to fit people everywhere, has handed on, in their place, to believers drawn from people everywhere the solemn worship of God in the way of Jesus. He, adorned not only with understanding but also with a divine endowment, overthrew the teaching about the demons on earth, who delight in incense and blood and the fumes that rise from the reek of sacrifice, and who, like the Titans or Giants of the myths, drag men down from the thought of God. Paying no heed himself to their plotting, though they plot most of all against the better sort, he laid down laws such that those who live by them will be blessed, never flattering the demons with sacrifices and wholly despising them because of the Word of God, who helps those who look upward and toward God.

And because God willed that the word of Jesus should prevail among men, the demons have been able to do nothing, though they have tried every means to see that there should be Christians no longer. For they stirred up those who reign, the senate, the governors everywhere, and even the peoples themselves, all of them unaware of the irrational and wicked working of the demons, against the word and those who believe in it. But the Word of God, mightier than all, even when hindered, taking the hindrance as food, so to speak, for its growth, went forward and spread over more and more souls; for God willed this.

Even if we have said this by way of digression, we have said it, I think, of necessity. For we wished to answer what Celsus says about the Jews, that, as he would have it, they were “runaways from Egypt,” and that these men, beloved of God, “never did anything worth mentioning.” And to the claim that they “were of no account or number,” we say that, as “a chosen race” and “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9; Exodus 19:6), withdrawing and avoiding mingling with the many so that their morals might not be corrupted, they were guarded by the divine power. They neither desired, as most men do, to win other kingdoms for themselves, nor were they forsaken, so as to become easy targets for plots because of their few numbers and, as far as their few numbers went, to perish utterly. And this held as long as they were still worthy of God’s protection. But when, as a whole nation that was sinning, they had to turn back to their God through hardships, they were forsaken, sometimes more and sometimes less, until, under the Romans, having committed the greatest sin in killing Jesus, they were forsaken completely.

title: The fathers named in prayers and spells
english: Next after this, Celsus, running over the contents of the first book of Moses, which is entitled Genesis, says that “they set about tracing their descent back to a first stock of sorcerers and deceivers, calling to witness faint and ambiguous sayings hidden away somewhere in darkness, and misinterpreting them to the ignorant and foolish; and this though, in all the long time before, no one had ever so much as laid claim to such a thing.” In these words he seems to me to have stated what he meant very obscurely. And it is likely that he contrived the obscurity of this passage on purpose, since he saw that the argument which establishes that the Jewish nation comes from these particular ancestors is strong; and yet, on the other hand, he did not want to seem ignorant of a matter concerning the Jews and their race that is not to be lightly dismissed.

It is clear, then, that the Jews trace their descent from the three fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Their names, joined to the title of God, have such power that the formula “the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:6) is used not only by those of that nation in their prayers to God and in charming away demons, but also by nearly all who busy themselves with spells and magic. For in magical writings this kind of invocation of God is found in many places, as is the use of the name of God as proper to these men, in dealings against the demons. These facts, then, which Jews and Christians bring forward as proof that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the fathers of the Jewish nation, were holy men, Celsus seems to me not to have been wholly ignorant of, and yet not to have set out clearly, since he could not answer the argument.

title: The patriarchs are known only from Genesis
english: For we put this question to all who use such invocations of God: “Tell us, sirs, who Abraham was, how great Isaac was, and what power Jacob had, that the title ‘God’, joined to their name, works such mighty deeds? From whom have you learned, or from whom can you learn, the facts about these men? And who took the trouble to write down their history, whether one that on its face exalts the men in secret writings, or one that by hidden meanings hints at great and wonderful things to those able to contemplate them?”

Then, when we ask and no one can show from what history at all the facts about these men come, whether Greek or barbarian, or not a history but some mystical record, we shall bring forward the book entitled Genesis, which contains the deeds of these men and God’s oracles to them. And we shall say: May it not be that the very fact that you too make use of the names of these three founders of the nation, because you see plainly that calling on them achieves results not to be despised, shows the divine character of these men? And we receive these men from no other source than the sacred books held among the Jews.

What is more, “the God of Israel” (Exodus 5:1), “the God of the Hebrews” (Exodus 3:18), and “the God who drowned the king of the Egyptians and the Egyptians in the Red Sea” (Exodus 14:27–28; 15:4) are often named and called upon against demons or certain wicked powers. And we learn the history of what is named, and the meaning of the names, from the Hebrews, who honour these things and tell of them in their ancestral writings and their ancestral language.

How then can the Jews, in trying to trace their descent from the first seed of these men, whom Celsus has supposed to be sorcerers and vagabonds, be shamelessly trying to trace themselves and their origin back to them, when the names of these men, being Hebrew, bear witness on behalf of the Hebrews, who have their sacred books in the Hebrew language and letters, that their nation is akin to these men? For even to this day the Jewish names, which belong to the Hebrew language, have been taken either from their writings or simply from what words mean in the Hebrew tongue.

title: Celsus asserts but never proves
english: And you who read Celsus’s writing, see whether it is not these things that his words hint at: “they set about tracing their descent back to a first stock of sorcerers and deceivers, calling to witness faint and ambiguous sayings hidden away somewhere in darkness.” For these names are hidden, and are not in the light or in the knowledge of the many. In our view they are not ambiguous, even if they are taken up by those who are strangers to our worship of God. But in the view of Celsus, who does not show what is ambiguous about the sayings, the charge has been tossed in, I do not know how.

Yet, if he wished to overturn fairly the genealogy which he thought the Jews, who boast of Abraham and his descendants, had most shamelessly adopted, he ought to have set out everything that bears on the subject. He ought first to have pleaded its case with whatever plausibility he thought it had, and after that to have overturned it nobly with what seemed to him the truth and with the arguments for that truth.

But neither Celsus nor anyone else, in treating the nature of names used for works of power, will be able to give an exact account of them and to prove that the men were contemptible whose very names have power not only among their own people but also among strangers.

He ought also to have shown how we deceive our hearers, as he supposes, by misinterpreting what concerns these names “to the ignorant and foolish”, while he himself, who boasts that he is neither ignorant nor foolish, gives the true interpretation of them.

He has also tossed in, in what he says about these names from which the Jews trace their descent, that never in all the long time before had there been any dispute over such names, but that now the Jews dispute about them with certain others, whom he did not name. Let anyone who wishes show who these claimants are, who argue against the Jews, with even some show of plausibility, that Jews and Christians do not give a sound report about the men to whom the names belong, while others are the ones who have grasped the wisest and truest things about them. But we are persuaded that no one will be able to do such a thing, since it is evident that the names have been taken from the Hebrew language, which is found among the Jews alone.

title: Hesiod came long after Moses
english: After this Celsus sets out material from history outside the divine word, about people who have laid claim to antiquity, such as the Athenians, Egyptians, Arcadians and Phrygians, who say that certain earth-born men arose among them, and each of whom offers proofs of it. And he says that “the Jews, huddled together in some corner of Palestine, utterly uneducated, and not having heard of these things sung long ago by Hesiod and countless other inspired men, put together a most incredible and tasteless tale: a man moulded by the hands of God and blown into (Genesis 2:7), a little woman made from his side (Genesis 2:21–22), commandments of God (Genesis 2:16–17), and a serpent working against these commandments, the serpent getting the better of God’s orders (Genesis 3:1–6). They tell a sort of myth, as if to old women, and most impiously make God weak from the very beginning, unable to persuade even the one man whom he himself had moulded.”

In these words the widely read and learned Celsus, who charges both Jews and Christians with ignorance and lack of education, plainly shows how accurately he knew the dates of each writer, Greek and barbarian! For he thinks that Hesiod and countless others, whom he calls inspired men, are older than Moses and his writings: Moses, who is shown to be much older than the Trojan War.

So it was not the Jews who put together a most incredible and tasteless tale about the earth-born man, but Celsus’s “inspired men”, Hesiod and his countless others. Having neither learned nor heard the far older and most venerable accounts in Palestine, they wrote such histories about the ancients as their theogonies too, ascribing birth to gods, so far as it lay with them, and countless other things.

With good reason, then, Plato expels from his commonwealth Homer and those who write such poems, as corrupters of the young (Plato, Republic 398a; 607a). Plato plainly did not think that those who left such poems behind were inspired men. But Celsus the Epicurean, who is better able to judge than Plato, if indeed he is the same man who composed two other books against the Christians, has perhaps, out of a wish to quarrel with us, called “inspired” those whom he did not think inspired.

title: The hands and the breath of God
english: He charges us with bringing in a man moulded by the hands of God, although the book of Genesis speaks of God’s hands neither at the making of man (Genesis 1:26–27) nor at his moulding (Genesis 2:7). It is Job and David who said, “Your hands made me and moulded me” (Job 10:8; Psalm 119:73). On these words “there is much to say” (Hebrews 5:11) in order to bring out what those who spoke them meant, not only about the difference between making and moulding but also about the hands of God.

Those who have not understood these hands, or similar expressions of the divine Scriptures, think that we ascribe to the God over all a shape such as the human shape. On their reasoning it would follow that we also think there are wings on God’s body, since the Scriptures about our God, taken literally, say this too (see Psalm 17:8; 91:4). But the present treatise does not require us to explain these things now; for we have examined them as our main subject, as far as we could, in our commentaries on Genesis.

Next, see Celsus’s malice in what follows. Our Scripture says of the moulding of man: “And he breathed into his face the breath of life, and the man became a living soul” (Genesis 2:7). But he, wishing maliciously to mock “he breathed into his face the breath of life”, though he has not even understood in what sense it was said, wrote that they put together “a man moulded by the hands of God and blown into”. He did this so that someone might suppose “blown into” was said in the way wineskins are blown up, and laugh at “he breathed into his face the breath of life”. Yet this was said figuratively and needs an explanation, one showing that God gave man a share of the incorruptible Spirit, as it is said: “Your incorruptible Spirit is in all things” (Wisdom of Solomon 12:1).

title: Hesiod’s Pandora and the woman from the rib
english: Then, since his set purpose was to speak ill of what is written, he also mocked the passage, “God cast a trance upon Adam, and he slept; and he took one of his ribs and filled up flesh in its place; and he built the rib which he had taken from Adam into a woman” (Genesis 2:21–22), and what follows. He did not even set out the wording, which could have made the hearer notice that it is spoken figuratively. And he would not even acknowledge that such things are taken as allegory, although later he says that the more reasonable of the Jews and Christians, ashamed of these things, try somehow to allegorize them.

One may say to him: Is it, then, that what your inspired Hesiod said about the woman in the form of a myth is taken as allegory, that she was given to men by Zeus as “an evil” “in return for fire” (Hesiod, Works and Days 57), while the woman taken from the rib of the man who slept after a “trance,” and built by God, seems to you to have been told without any meaning and without any hidden sense? But it is not fair-minded to refrain from laughing at those verses as a myth, and to admire them as philosophy told in a myth, and yet to sneer at these words, resting the mind on the wording alone, and to think that they will turn out to mean nothing. For if one must find fault with things said under hidden meanings because of the bare wording, see whether it is not rather Hesiod’s verses that will incur laughter, though he was, as you say, an inspired man, and wrote such things as these:

“Then Zeus the cloud-gatherer, in anger, said to him: ‘Son of Iapetus, you who know counsels beyond all others, you rejoice that you stole fire and outwitted my mind, a great sorrow for yourself and for men who are to come. To them, in return for fire, I will give an evil in which all may delight in their hearts, embracing their own evil.’ So he spoke; and the father of men and gods brought it to pass. He bade far-famed Hephaestus with all speed to mix earth with water, and to put in it a human voice and strength, and to make it like the immortal gods in face, a maiden’s fair and lovely form; and he bade Athena teach her crafts, to weave the richly worked web; and golden Aphrodite to shed grace about her head, and painful longing and cares that wear out the limbs; and to put in her the mind of a dog and a thievish nature he charged Hermes, the guide, the slayer of Argus. So he spoke; and they obeyed Zeus, the lord, the son of Cronus. At once the famous lame god moulded from earth the likeness of a modest maiden, by the counsels of the son of Cronus; the goddess, grey-eyed Athena, girded and adorned her; about her the divine Graces and queenly Persuasion set golden necklaces upon her skin, and the lovely-haired Seasons crowned her with spring flowers; and Pallas Athena fitted every ornament to her body.
