And in her breast the guide, the slayer of Argus, wrought lies and wheedling words and a thievish nature, by the counsels of loud-thundering Zeus; and the herald of the gods put a voice in her, and named this woman Pandora, because all who have their homes on Olympus gave her as a gift, a sorrow to men who eat bread” (Hesiod, Works and Days 53–82).

Laughable on its face, too, is what is said about the jar: “For before this the tribes of men lived on the earth far from evils, without hard toil and painful diseases, which bring men their dooms. But the woman lifted the great lid from the jar with her hands and scattered them, and devised grievous sorrows for men. Hope alone remained there within, in an unbreakable house, under the lip of the jar, and did not fly out of the door; for before that she had put the lid on the jar” (Hesiod, Works and Days 90–98).

To the man who solemnly allegorizes these things, whether he succeeds in the allegory or not, we will say: Is it only the Greeks who may philosophize under a hidden meaning, and the Egyptians as well, and those of the barbarians who pride themselves on mysteries and on truth, while the Jews alone, with their lawgiver and their writers, seemed to you the most senseless of all men, and this nation alone has received no share of any power of God, the nation that was taught, in so lofty a way, to rise up to the uncreated nature of God, to fix its gaze on him alone, and to look for its hopes from him alone?

title: Plato’s garden of Zeus and the paradise of God
english: Celsus also lampoons the story of the serpent, as one who works against God’s commands to man (Genesis 3:1–5), and supposes the account to be a myth like the tales that old women pass on. He deliberately did not name God’s “paradise,” nor say how “God” is said to have planted it “in Eden toward the east” (Genesis 2:8), and then to have made spring up “out of the ground every tree beautiful to see and good for food, and the tree of life in the middle of the paradise, and the tree of knowing good and evil” (Genesis 2:9), with what is said after these words, which could of themselves move a well-disposed reader to see that all this is expressed in figures, and not unworthily. Since he has done this, come, let us set beside it what Socrates says about Love in Plato’s Symposium, words which Plato gave to Socrates as more dignified than those of all who spoke about Love in the Symposium. Plato’s wording runs as follows:

“When Aphrodite was born, the gods held a feast, and among the rest was Resource, the son of Cunning. When they had dined, Poverty came to beg, as one does when there is feasting, and she was about the doors. Now Resource, drunk with nectar (for there was not yet wine), went into the garden of Zeus and, weighed down, fell asleep. Poverty, then, because of her own lack of resource, plotted to have a child by Resource; she lay down beside him and conceived Love. That is why Love has become the follower and attendant of Aphrodite, since he was begotten at her birthday feast, and also because he is by nature a lover of the beautiful, and Aphrodite is beautiful. Since Love, then, is the son of Resource and Poverty, his lot is this. First, he is always poor, and far from being tender and beautiful, as most people think, he is hard and parched, barefoot and homeless. He always lies on the ground, without bedding, sleeping in doorways and on the roads under the open sky; having his mother’s nature, he always lives with want. But after his father again he lays plots for the beautiful and the good. He is brave, headlong and intense, a formidable hunter, always weaving some scheme, eager for understanding and full of resource, philosophizing all through his life, a formidable enchanter, sorcerer and sophist. By nature he is neither immortal nor mortal: at one time on the same day he flourishes and lives, when he has plenty, and at another he dies, and comes to life again through his father’s nature. But what he gains is always slipping away, so that Love is never either destitute or rich. And again he is in the middle between wisdom and ignorance” (Plato, Symposium 203b–e).

Now, if those who read this imitate Celsus’s malice (far be that from Christians), they will laugh at the myth and make a mockery of so great a man as Plato. But if, examining philosophically what is said in the form of a myth, they are able to find Plato’s purpose […]: how he managed to hide, for the sake of the many, the doctrines that seemed great to him under the form of a myth, and yet to speak, as he had to, to those who know how to find, from myths, what the author of these things meant about the truth.

I have set out this myth from Plato because of “the garden of Zeus” in it, which seems to have some likeness to the paradise of God; and because of Poverty, who may be compared with the serpent there; and because of Resource, plotted against by Poverty, who may be compared with the man plotted against by the serpent. It is not at all clear whether Plato came upon these things by chance, or whether, as some think, on his journey to Egypt he met also those who study the philosophy of the Jews, learned some things from them, and kept some while altering others, taking care not to offend the Greeks by keeping wholly to the wisdom of the Jews, a people in bad repute with the many because of the strangeness of their laws and their peculiar way of life.

But this was not the time to explain either Plato’s myth or the story of the serpent and of God’s paradise and all that is recorded to have taken place in it; for we dealt with these matters as our main subject, as well as we could, in our commentaries on Genesis.

title: Adam is every man
english: When he says that “the story of Moses most impiously brings in God as weak straight away, from the very beginning, and unable to persuade even one man whom he himself had formed,” to this too we shall say that the charge is like a complaint against the existence of wickedness, which God has not been able to prevent even in a single man, so that at least one man might be found who from the beginning had never tasted wickedness. For just as those who care to defend providence make their defence on this point with arguments neither few nor contemptible, so too those will philosophize about Adam and his sin who know that the name Adam, in Greek, is “man,” and that in what seems to be about Adam, Moses is giving an account of the nature of man.

For “in Adam,” as the word says, “all die” (1 Corinthians 15:22), and they were condemned “in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Romans 5:14), the divine word saying these things not so much of one particular man as of the whole race. Indeed, in the sequence of what is said as though of one man, the curse of Adam is common to all (Genesis 3:17–19); and as for what is said against the woman, there is no woman of whom it is not said (Genesis 3:16). And the man who is cast out of paradise with the woman (Genesis 3:23–24), clothed in the “garments of skins” (Genesis 3:21) which, because of the transgression of humankind, God made for those who had sinned, holds a secret and mystical meaning, beyond the descent of the soul as Plato tells it, which sheds its wings and is carried down here “until it lays hold of something solid” (Plato, Phaedrus 246c).

title: The ark is no strange tale
english: Next he says this: “Then a flood, and a strange ark with everything inside it (Genesis 6:14–7:16), and a dove and a crow as messengers (Genesis 8:6–12), counterfeiting and tampering with the story of Deucalion. For I do not suppose they expected that these things would come to light; they simply told myths to little children.”

Here too, see the man’s unphilosophical hatred of the most ancient Scripture of the Jews. For he could find nothing to say against the story of the flood, and he did not notice what he could have said against the ark and its measurements: that if one takes, as the many do, the statement of “three hundred cubits” for the length “of the ark,” “and fifty” for the breadth, “and thirty” for the height (Genesis 6:15), it was not possible to claim that it held the animals of the earth, the clean by fourteen of each kind and the unclean by four (Genesis 7:2–3). Instead he simply said “strange, with everything inside.”

For what is strange about it, when the record says it was a hundred years in the making, and narrowed from the three hundred cubits of its length and the fifty of its breadth until the thirty cubits of its height ended in a single cubit of length and breadth (Genesis 6:16)? Why was the structure not rather a marvel, like a very great city, since its measurements are given as squares, so that its length at the base is ninety thousand and its breadth two thousand five hundred? Why should one not admire the design that made it firmly braced and able to withstand a storm that brought on a flood? For it was smeared not with pitch or any other such material, but solidly with asphalt (Genesis 6:14). And is it not a marvel that, by the providence of God, embers of life of every kind were brought inside, so that the earth might again have the seeds of all living creatures (Genesis 7:3), God making use of a most righteous man (Genesis 6:9), who was to be the father of those who came after the flood?

title: The dove, the raven and the charge of forgery
english: Celsus has tossed in the matter of the dove so as to seem to have read the book of Genesis, though he could say nothing to prove that the story of the dove is a fiction (Genesis 8:8–12). Then, since it is his habit to reword what is written so as to make it more laughable, he has changed “the raven” into a crow (Genesis 8:7), and he thinks that Moses recorded these things while tampering with the story of Deucalion told among the Greeks, unless perhaps he does not even think the writing is by Moses, but by a number of people. For that is what these words show: “counterfeiting and tampering with the story of Deucalion,” and these as well: “For I do not suppose they expected that these things would come to light.”

But how could those who gave writings to a whole nation not expect them to come to light, when they even prophesied that this worship of God would be preached to all the nations? And when Jesus said to the Jews, “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matthew 21:43), what else was he arranging but that he himself, by divine power, should bring into the light the whole of the Jewish Scripture, which contains mysteries of the kingdom of God? Then, if they read the theogonies of the Greeks and the stories about the twelve gods, they lend them dignity by allegories; but when they wish to mock ours, they say these were simply told as myths to little children.

title: The patriarchs’ troubles and Jacob’s marked flocks
english: He speaks of “a most absurd and untimely begetting of children”; although he has not named it, he clearly means that of Abraham and Sarah (Genesis 18:11–14; Genesis 21:1–2). And when he tosses in “the plots of brothers,” he means either Cain plotting against Abel (Genesis 4:8) or, besides him, Esau against Jacob as well (Genesis 27:41); and by “a father’s grief” perhaps Isaac’s at Jacob’s going away, and perhaps also Jacob’s over Joseph, who was sold into Egypt (Genesis 37:28; Genesis 37:34–35). And in writing of “the treacheries of mothers,” I think he means Rebekah, who contrived that Isaac’s prayers should reach Jacob first, and not Esau (Genesis 27:5–29).

If we say that God shared most closely in the life of all these, what absurdity do we commit, since we are convinced that he never withdraws his own divinity from those who have devoted themselves to him and live nobly and with vigour?

He has mocked the wealth Jacob gained while with Laban, not understanding what the words refer to: “And the unmarked were Laban’s, and the marked were Jacob’s” (Genesis 30:42). And he says that God “gave his sons little donkeys and little sheep and camels”; and he did not see that “all these things happened to them as figures, and were written for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Corinthians 10:11). Among us, characters of many colours, made “marked” by the word of God, live as citizens, given as a possession to him who is figuratively called Jacob. For those from the nations who believe in him were signified by what is written about Laban and Jacob.

title: The wells of the righteous and Paul’s allegory
english: Far from grasping the intent of what is written, he says that God also “gave wells to the righteous.” For he did not observe that the righteous do not build cisterns but dig “wells” (Genesis 26:18–22), seeking to find the spring that lies within and the source of good things fit to drink, since they also take in a figurative sense the commandment that says: “Drink waters from your own vessels and from the spring of your own wells. Let not your waters overflow outside your own spring, but let your waters pass through into your streets. Let them be yours alone, and let no stranger share them with you” (Proverbs 5:15–17).

In many places the word has made use of events that really happened and recorded them to set forth greater things, conveyed by a hidden sense. Of this kind are the passages about wells, and about the marriages and the various unions of the righteous; someone will more fittingly try to make these clear in commentaries on those very passages. That wells were indeed built by the righteous in the land of the Philistines, as is recorded in Genesis (Genesis 26:15–18), is plain from the wonderful wells shown at Ascalon, which are worthy of note because their construction is strange and unlike that of other wells.

That brides and maidservants are to be taken in a figurative sense is not our own teaching; we have received it from wise men of old. One of them said, stirring his hearer to figurative interpretation: “Tell me, you who read the law, do you not hear the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman. But the son of the slave woman was born according to the flesh, the son of the free woman through the promise. These things are spoken in allegory: for these women are two covenants, one from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery, which is Hagar” (Galatians 4:21–24); and a little later: “But the Jerusalem above,” he says, “is free, which is our mother” (Galatians 4:26). Whoever cares to take up the Epistle to the Galatians will learn in what way the passages about the marriages and the unions with maidservants have been allegorised; for the word wishes us too to imitate not what are thought to be the bodily acts of those who did these things, but, as the apostles of Jesus are accustomed to call them, the spiritual ones.

title: Lot and his daughters
english: He ought to have welcomed the love of truth in those who wrote the divine Scriptures, who did not hide even what is unseemly, and so been led to accept the rest too, even the more marvellous things, as not invented. But he has done the opposite: the story of Lot and his daughters (Genesis 19:30–38), which he neither examined according to the letter nor searched out by its higher sense, he called “more lawless than the crimes of Thyestes.”

Now there is no need to speak at present of the figurative sense of the passage: what Sodom is, and what is meant by the word of the angels to the man escaping from there, when they say, “Do not look behind you, nor stop anywhere in the whole surrounding region; escape to the mountain, lest you too be swept away” (Genesis 19:17); and who Lot is, and who his wife, who became “a pillar of salt” (Genesis 19:26) because she turned back; and who his daughters are, who made their father drunk so as to become mothers by him (Genesis 19:32–36).

But come, let us in a few words ease what seems unseemly in the story taken literally. The Greeks too inquired into the nature of things good, evil and indifferent; and those of them who hit the mark place good and evil in the will alone, and say that all things considered apart from the will are, in their own nature, indifferent, but that the will, when it uses these as it ought, is praiseworthy, and when it does not, blameworthy. So they have said, in their treatment of indifferent things, that in its own nature intercourse with daughters is indifferent, even though one must not do such a thing in established societies. And by way of hypothesis, to show that such a thing is indifferent, they have taken the case of a wise man left alone with his daughter after the whole human race has been destroyed, and they ask whether the father will fittingly come together with his daughter, so that, on that very hypothesis, the whole human race may not perish.

Is this, then, soundly said among the Greeks, with the far from contemptible school of the Stoics arguing for it? And when young girls who have heard of the burning of the world but have not understood it clearly see fire spreading over their city and their land (Genesis 19:24–25), and, supposing that an ember of the human race has been left in their father and themselves (Genesis 19:31), wish on that supposition to found the world again, will they be worse than the wise man of the Stoics’ hypothesis, who fittingly comes together with his daughters when all mankind has perished?

I am not unaware that some, offended at the intention of Lot’s daughters, have judged the deed unholy, and have said that from unholy unions accursed nations were born, the Moabites and the Ammonites (Genesis 19:37–38). And indeed the divine Scripture is not found clearly approving such a deed as well done, nor charging and blaming it. But however the event stands, it is taken up into a figurative sense, and it also has some defence in itself.

title: What Celsus leaves out about Joseph
english: Celsus tosses in besides “the hatred,” I suppose of Esau toward Jacob (Genesis 27:41), a man acknowledged in Scripture to be base. And without setting out clearly the story of Simeon and Levi, who avenged the outrage done to their sister when she was violated by the son of the king of Shechem (Genesis 34:1–31), he accuses them. He speaks of “brothers selling,” meaning the sons of Jacob, and “a brother being sold,” meaning Joseph, and “a father deceived,” meaning Jacob, since he suspected nothing of his sons when they showed him Joseph’s “many-coloured coat” (Genesis 37:32), but believed them and “mourned” for Joseph as lost while he was a slave in Egypt (Genesis 37:33–35).

But see how Celsus has gathered material from the history in hatred and not in love of truth. So, where the history seemed to him to contain grounds for accusation, he sets it out; but where it gives a notable display of chastity, when Joseph did not yield to the passion of the woman held to be his mistress, who now pleaded with him and now threatened him (Genesis 39:7–20), he did not so much as mention the history. For we would see that Joseph was far nobler than anything told of Bellerophon, since he chose to be shut up in prison rather than lose a chaste mind. Indeed, though he could have defended himself and argued his case against the woman who accused him, he kept a noble silence, entrusting his cause to God.

title: Joseph’s rise and the going out from Egypt
english: After this Celsus, for form’s sake and very obscurely, recalls the dreams of the chief cupbearer and the chief baker and of Pharaoh, and their interpretation (Genesis 40:1–41:36), as a result of which Joseph was brought out of prison and entrusted by Pharaoh with the second throne over the Egyptians (Genesis 41:14; Genesis 41:40–43). What absurdity, then, did the account of the history contain, even taken by itself, that he should set it down as part of his accusation, he who gave the title True Doctrine to a book that sets out no doctrines but accuses Christians and Jews?

He also says that the one who had been sold did things as a favour to the brothers who sold him, when they were starving and had been sent with their donkeys to trade (Genesis 42:1–3; Genesis 42:26), though Celsus does not even make clear what these things were. He sets down the recognition as well (Genesis 45:1–15), with what purpose I do not know, or what absurdity he means to point out in the recognition. For not even Momus himself, so to speak, could reasonably find fault with these things, which even apart from their figurative sense have great appeal.

He also sets down that Joseph, who had been sold as a slave, was set free and returned in procession to his father’s tomb (Genesis 50:7–13), and he thinks the account contains grounds for accusation, saying: “by whom” (that is, plainly, Joseph) “the splendid and godlike race of the Jews, spread abroad in great numbers in Egypt, was ordered to live as aliens somewhere outside and to tend flocks in despised places.” And out of his own hostile disposition he has added that they were ordered to tend flocks in despised places, without showing how Goshen, the district of Egypt, is despised (Genesis 46:34; Genesis 47:6). And he called the departure of the people from Egypt a flight, without so much as recalling what is written in Exodus about the departure of the Hebrews from the land of Egypt (Exodus 12:31–42).

We have set these things out as well, to show that Celsus placed under the heading of accusation and idle talk even things that do not appear, even according to the letter, to deserve accusation, without establishing by argument what he thinks is bad in our Scripture.

title: The shameful myths are the Greeks’ own
english: Then, like a man who has given himself over to nothing but hatred and hostility toward the teaching of Jews and Christians, he says that “the more reasonable among both Jews and Christians allegorize these things.” He says that “being ashamed of them, they take refuge in allegory.” One might answer him: if myths and fictions, whether written with a hidden meaning or in any other way at all, are to be called shameful when taken in their first sense, to which should this be said to apply if not to the stories of the Greeks? In them sons who are gods castrate fathers who are gods, and fathers who are gods swallow sons who are gods; a goddess mother hands the father “of men and gods” (Homer, Iliad 1.544) a stone in place of her son; a father has intercourse with his daughter; and a wife binds her husband, taking as her helpers in the binding the brother of the one being bound and his daughter (Homer, Iliad 1.399–400).

And why need I list the absurd stories of the Greeks about the gods, which are plainly shameful even when they are allegorized? Why, Chrysippus of Soli, who is thought to have adorned the Stoa of the philosophers with many intelligent writings, gives a false interpretation of the painting at Samos in which Hera was painted doing an unspeakable act with Zeus. For this venerable philosopher says in his writings that matter has received the seminal principles of god and holds them in itself for the ordering of the universe; for in the painting at Samos Hera is matter and Zeus is god.

It is for these reasons, and because of such myths and countless others, that we are unwilling to call the God over all “Zeus” even in name, or the sun “Apollo,” or the moon “Artemis.” Rather, practising pure piety toward the Creator and speaking well of his beautiful works, we do not defile divine things even in their names. In this we accept the words of Plato in the Philebus, where he would not accept pleasure as a goddess: “For my fear, Protarchus,” he says, “concerning the names of the gods is of this kind” (Plato, Philebus 12c). We, then, truly have “fear” concerning the name of God and of his beautiful works, so that we do not accept any myth, even on the pretext of a figurative meaning, to the harm of the young.

title: The writers of Scripture read it figuratively
english: If Celsus had read the Scripture without prejudice, he would not have said that our writings “are not such as to admit allegory.” For from the prophecies, in which events drawn from history are written, but not as history, one may be led to see that the histories too were written with a figurative meaning as their aim, and were arranged with the greatest wisdom, with regard both for the multitude of those who believe more simply and for the few who wish, or are even able, to examine matters with understanding. And if it were those among Jews and Christians today whom Celsus counts reasonable who allegorized what is written, Celsus might perhaps be thought to be saying something plausible. But since the fathers and writers of the doctrines themselves interpret such things figuratively, what else is one to suppose than that they were written so as to be read figuratively in their primary sense?

We shall set out a few passages out of very many, to show that Celsus slanders the Scriptures in vain as incapable of admitting allegory. Paul, the apostle of Jesus, says: “It is written in the law, ‘You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain’ (Deuteronomy 25:4). Is it for oxen that God cares? Or does he speak entirely for our sake? It was written for our sake, because the one who ploughs ought to plough in hope, and the one who threshes ought to thresh in hope of a share” (1 Corinthians 9:9–10). And elsewhere the same apostle says: “For it is written, ‘For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh’ (Genesis 2:24). This mystery is great; but I speak with reference to Christ and to the church” (Ephesians 5:31–32). And again in another place: “We know that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:1–2).

Then, interpreting the story of the manna (Exodus 16:14–15) and the account of the water that is recorded to have come miraculously out of a rock (Exodus 17:6; Numbers 20:11), he says this: “And all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank from a spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:3–4). And Asaph, showing that the histories in Exodus and Numbers are “riddles” and “parables,” as is written in the book of Psalms, begins in this way when he is about to recall them: “Pay attention, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth. I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter riddles from of old, such things as we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us” (Psalm 78:1–3).

title: The prophet prays to see the hidden things
english: Moreover, if the law of Moses had contained nothing written in it to be made known through hidden meanings, the prophet would not have said to God in his prayer: “Uncover my eyes, and I shall perceive your wonders out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). But as it is, he knew that a “veil” of ignorance lies upon the heart of those who read but do not understand what is said figuratively (2 Corinthians 3:15). This “veil is taken away” (2 Corinthians 3:16) as God’s gift, when he hears the one who has done all that lay in his power, who by practice has trained his senses to distinguish good and evil (Hebrews 5:14), and who says again and again in prayer: “Uncover my eyes, and I shall perceive your wonders out of your law” (Psalm 119:18).

Who, reading of a dragon that lives in the river of Egypt, and of fish lurking in its scales (Ezekiel 29:3–4), or of the mountains of Egypt filled “with the dung” of Pharaoh (Ezekiel 32:6), is not moved at once to ask who it is that fills the mountains of the Egyptians with so much of his foul-smelling “dung,” and what the mountains of the Egyptians are? And what are the rivers in Egypt about which this same Pharaoh boasts, saying, “The rivers are mine, and I made them” (Ezekiel 29:3)? And who is the dragon that corresponds to those rivers, as the interpretation will show them to be, and who are the fish in its scales?

But why need I establish further what needs no establishing? Of such things it is said: “Who is wise, and will understand these things? Or who is discerning, and will know them?” (Hosea 14:9). I have extended my argument at some length because I wished to show that Celsus was not right in saying that “the more reasonable among Jews and Christians try somehow to allegorize these things, but they are not such as to admit any allegory; they are plainly fables of the silliest kind.” For it is the stories of the Greeks, far more, that are fables, and not only of the silliest kind but also of the most impious. For our writings have had regard also for the multitude of simpler people, and this the makers of the Greek fictions did not take care to do. That is why Plato, with good reason, banishes such myths and such poems from his own republic (Plato, Republic 2.377b–3.398b).

title: Philo, Aristobulus and Numenius
english: He also seems to me to have heard that there are writings containing allegories of the law. If he had read them, he would not have said: “At any rate, the allegories that are thought to have been written about them are far more shameful and absurd than the myths, for they join together, with an astonishing and utterly senseless folly, things that can in no way whatever be fitted together.” He seems to say this about the writings of Philo, or even of men still more ancient, such as the writings of Aristobulus. But I conjecture that Celsus has not read these books, since in many places they seem to me so successful that even the philosophers among the Greeks would be won over by what they say. In them not only is the style carefully worked, but so also are the thoughts, the doctrines, and the use made of what Celsus takes to be myths from the Scriptures.

I know also of Numenius the Pythagorean, a man who expounded Plato far better and who championed the doctrines of the Pythagoreans. In many places in his writings he sets out passages of Moses and the prophets and gives them a figurative interpretation that is not unpersuasive, as in the work called The Hoopoe, and in the books On Numbers and On Place. In the third book On the Good he even sets out a story about Jesus, without saying his name, and interprets it figuratively; whether successfully or not is a question for another time. He also sets out the story about Moses and Jannes and Jambres (Exodus 7:11; 2 Timothy 3:8). We do not take pride in that; but we do welcome him more than Celsus and other Greeks, because out of love of learning he was willing to examine our writings as well, and was moved by them as writings to be read figuratively and not as foolish ones.

title: The dialogue of Jason and Papiscus
english: Next after this, Celsus picks out, from all the writings that contain allegories and narratives in a style that is not to be despised, the humblest one, a work that can contribute something toward faith for the many and simpler people but is certainly not able to move the more intelligent. He says: “Such, for example, is a disputation between a certain Papiscus and Jason that I have come across, which deserves not laughter but rather pity and hatred. It is not my purpose, then, to refute these things; for they are plain to everyone, I suppose, especially if anyone will be patient and bear to listen to the writings themselves. I would rather teach the nature of things: that God made nothing mortal, but the works of God are all the things that are immortal, and mortal things are the works of those immortal beings. The soul is the work of God, but the body is of another nature. And in this respect the body of a bat, or of a maggot, or of a frog, will not differ at all from that of a human being; for the matter is the same, and what is perishable in them is alike.”

Nevertheless, I should like anyone whatever who has heard Celsus speaking so vehemently, and declaring that the writing entitled Disputation of Jason and Papiscus concerning Christ deserves not laughter but hatred, to take this little treatise in his hands and be patient and bear to listen to what is in it, so that he may condemn Celsus at once, since he will find nothing in the book that deserves hatred. If anyone reads it without prejudice, he will find that the book does not even move one to laughter. In it a Christian is recorded arguing with a Jew from the Jewish Scriptures and showing that the prophecies about the Christ fit Jesus; though the other, in the role of the Jew, holds his ground against the argument in a way that is neither ignoble nor unfitting.

title: Pity and hatred cannot go together
english: I do not know how Celsus could bring together things that do not mix and that by nature cannot occur at the same time in human nature, and say that the book deserves pity and hatred. For everyone will agree that someone who is pitied is not hated while he is pitied, and someone who is hated is not pitied while he is hated. Celsus says that it is not his purpose to refute these things, because he thinks they are plain to everyone even before any reasoned refutation is brought against them, as worthless and deserving of pity and hatred. But we urge the reader of this defence, written against Celsus’s accusation, to bear with our writings and listen to them, and, as far as he can, to infer from what is written the purpose of those who wrote it, their conscience, and their disposition. For he will find men who contend ardently for what they have come to believe, and some who make it clear that they are recording a story they had seen and understood, as something marvellous and worth writing down for the benefit of those who were to hear it.

Or let someone dare to say that it is not the source and beginning of every benefit to believe in the God of the universe, to do everything with a view to pleasing him in every matter whatever, and not even to think of anything that displeases him, since not only our words and deeds but even our thoughts will be judged. And what other teaching could more forcefully lead human nature to live well than faith, or the conviction, that the God over all watches over everything we say and do, and even what we think? Let anyone who wishes compare with it another way that both converts and improves, not just one or two people, but as many as possible, so that by comparing the two ways one may understand exactly which teaching disposes people toward the good.

title: Celsus declares but does not teach
english: In the passage of Celsus that I set out, which paraphrases certain things from the Timaeus (Plato, Timaeus 41a–d), it is written that God made nothing mortal, but only immortal things, while mortal things are the works of others; that “the soul is the work of God, but the body is of another nature”; and that a man’s body will differ in nothing from the body of a bat or a maggot or a frog, “for the matter is the same, and what is perishable in them is alike.” Come, then, let us discuss these points too for a little while. We shall be refuting a man who either does not acknowledge his own Epicurean opinion, or, as someone might say, later changed over to better views, or even, as another might say, is a namesake of the Epicurean.

For in declaring such things, having set out to speak against not only us but also the far from contemptible school of philosophers who follow Zeno of Citium, he ought to have proved that the bodies of living creatures are not works of God, and that the great skill shown in them did not come from the first Mind. So too with the countless plants of every kind, which are governed by an indwelling nature that has no sense-impressions, and which came into being to serve a use of no small account in the universe, for men and for the animals that serve men, whatever else may be true of them: he ought not only to have declared but also to have taught that it was not some perfect mind that implanted so many qualities in the matter of plants.

And if once he made gods the craftsmen of all bodies, on the ground that the soul alone is God’s work, how would it not have been consistent for one who divides up so many works of craft and assigns them to many to establish, with some argument of real weight, differences among the gods: some fashioning the bodies of men, others, let us say, those of cattle, and others those of wild beasts? Seeing gods as the craftsmen of serpents and asps and basilisks, some of them makers of each particular species of these, and others makers of the species of each plant and each herb, he ought to have stated the reasons for these divisions. For perhaps, had he given himself to examining the questions of this topic with precision, he would either have held to one God, the Maker of all, who made each thing for some end and for the sake of something; or, if he did not hold to this, he would have seen what defence he must make about the perishable, a thing indifferent in its own nature, and that there is nothing absurd in a world composed of unlike things having come into being from one Craftsman, who fashions the differences of species for the good of the whole.

Or at the very least he ought not to have pronounced on so great a doctrine at all, if he was not going to prove what he professed to teach. Unless, perhaps, the man who blames those who profess bare faith wanted us ourselves to believe what he declared, even though what he professed was not to declare but to teach.

title: What Moses wrote of the making of the world
english: I am not yet saying that, if he had, as he puts it, “been patient and borne to listen to the writings” of Moses and the prophets, he would have noticed why the words “God made” are applied to heaven and earth (Genesis 1:1), and to what is called the firmament (Genesis 1:7), and further to the lights and the stars (Genesis 1:16); after these to the great sea creatures and every soul “of creeping living things, which the waters brought forth according to their kinds,” and every winged bird “according to its kind” (Genesis 1:21); next to the wild beasts “of the earth according to their kind,” and the cattle “according to their kind,” and all the creeping things “of the earth according to their kind” (Genesis 1:25); and last of all to man (Genesis 1:27). But “made” is not said of other things. For light, the text is content with “light came to be” (Genesis 1:3); and for the gathering into one of all the water beneath the whole heaven, with “it was so” (Genesis 1:9). It is the same with the things that sprouted from the earth, when “the earth brought forth plants of grass, sowing seed according to their kind and likeness, and the fruit-bearing tree yielding fruit whose seed is in it, according to its kind, on the earth” (Genesis 1:12).

He would also have asked to whom, whether to one or to more than one, the written commands of God about the coming into being of each part of the world were spoken. And he would not lightly have accused, as unintelligible and holding no hidden meaning, what was written here either by Moses or, as we would say, by the divine Spirit in Moses, by whom he also prophesied. For Moses knew “the things that are, the things that will be, and the things that were before” (Homer, Iliad 1.70) better than the seers whom the poets speak of as having known them.

title: The same matter underlies the heavens
english: Further, Celsus says: “The soul is the work of God, but the body is of another nature. And in this respect the body of a bat or a maggot or a frog or a man will differ in nothing; for the matter is the same, and what is perishable in them is alike.” To this argument of his too we must reply: if, because the same matter underlies the body of a bat or a maggot or a frog or a man, these bodies will differ in nothing from one another, then clearly the bodies of these creatures will differ in nothing from the sun or the moon or the stars or heaven, or from any other of those that the Greeks call gods perceived by the senses. For the same matter underlies all bodies, and by its own definition it is without quality and without shape. From whom it receives its qualities, on Celsus’s view, since he will not have anything perishable be a work of God, I do not know. For by Celsus’s own argument what is perishable in anything whatever that has come into being from the same underlying matter must be alike.

Unless, perhaps, hard pressed at this point, Celsus will leap away from Plato, who makes the soul out of a kind of mixing bowl (Plato, Timaeus 41d), and take refuge with Aristotle and the Peripatetics, who say that the ether is immaterial and is of a fifth nature beside the four elements. Against this argument both the followers of Plato and those of the Stoa have taken a stand, and done so with credit. And we too, whom Celsus despises, shall take a stand against it, since we are called upon to explain and establish what is said in the prophet as follows: “The heavens will perish, but you will remain; and they will all grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will roll them up, and they will be changed. But you are the same” (Psalm 102:26–27). Still, even these points are enough against Celsus, who declared that “The soul is the work of God, but the body is of another nature.” From his argument it followed that the body of a bat or a maggot or a frog differs in nothing from the ethereal body.

title: Matter takes the qualities God wills
english: See, then, whether we should side with a man who brings such doctrines to his accusation of Christians, and abandon the argument that allows a difference among bodies because of the qualities laid upon bodies and found in them. For we too know that there are “both heavenly bodies and earthly bodies,” and that the “glory” of “heavenly” bodies is one thing and that of “earthly” bodies another (1 Corinthians 15:40); nor is it the same even among the “heavenly” ones, for “the glory of the sun is one thing, and the glory of the stars another,” and among the stars themselves “star differs from star in glory” (1 Corinthians 15:41). That is why, since we accept the resurrection “of the dead,” we say that changes take place in the qualities that are in bodies. For some of them, sown “in corruption, are raised in incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15:42); sown “in dishonour, are raised in glory”; and sown “in weakness, are raised in power” (1 Corinthians 15:43); and bodies sown natural are raised spiritual (1 Corinthians 15:44).

All of us who have accepted providence establish that the underlying matter can receive whatever qualities the Creator wills. By God’s will there is now such-and-such a quality in this matter, and afterwards another, let us say, better and different. There are also fixed courses for the changes in bodies, from the time the world has existed and for as long as it exists — whether a new and different course will take their place after the destruction of the world, which our writings call the consummation (Matthew 24:3), I do not know. Since that is so, it is no wonder if at present, as most people say, a serpent arises from a dead man, reshaped out of his spinal marrow, and a bee from an ox, a wasp from a horse, a beetle from an ass, and, in short, worms from most things. Celsus thinks this proves that none of these is a work of God, and that the qualities, ordered from I know not where so that these arise from those, are not the work of some divine reason that changes the qualities in matter.

title: Which soul is God’s work?
english: We say this further to Celsus, who said, “The soul is the work of God, but the body is of another nature,” and who tossed out so great a doctrine not only without proof but also without drawing distinctions; for he did not make clear whether every soul is God’s work or only the rational soul. So we say to him: if every soul is God’s work, then clearly the souls of irrational and utterly worthless creatures are so too, so that every body as well is of another nature than the soul. And indeed in what follows, where he says that irrational animals are dearer to God than we are and have a purer notion of the divine, he seems to represent not only the soul of men but much more the soul of irrational animals as God’s work; for this follows from saying that they are dearer to God than we are.

But if only the rational soul is God’s work, then, first, he did not make this clear; and second, from his having spoken of the soul without distinction, taken to mean that not every soul but only the rational soul is God’s work, it follows that not every body is of another nature either. And if not every body is of another nature, but the body of each living creature corresponds to its soul, clearly the body of a creature whose soul is God’s work would differ from a body in which there dwells a soul that is not God’s work. And so it will be false that the body of a bat or a maggot or a frog will differ in nothing from that of a man.

title: Bodies differ by those who dwell in them
english: For it is absurd that stones should be thought purer or more defiled than other stones, and buildings than other buildings, according as they were built for the honour of the divine or to receive the most dishonoured and accursed bodies, while bodies are held not to differ from bodies according as those who have dwelt in them are rational or irrational, and, among rational beings, according as they are the more virtuous or the worst of men. Indeed, this is what has led some to dare to deify the bodies of eminent men, as having received a virtuous soul, and to cast out or dishonour the bodies of the worst. Not that this has been done altogether soundly; but it took its beginning from a sound notion. Or will the wise man, after the death of Anytus and Socrates, take the same care over the burial of the body of Socrates as over that of Anytus, and build a like mound or tomb for both?

We have said these things because of the phrase “none of which is a work of God.” The “which” refers to the body of a man, or to the serpents that come from that body; to the body of an ox, or to the bees that come from an ox’s body; and to the body of a horse or an ass, and to the wasps that come from a horse and the beetles that come from an ass. Because of these words we were compelled to take up again the saying too: “The soul is the work of God, but the body is of another nature.”

title: One nature shared by all bodies
english: Next he says that “the nature of all the bodies named above is common, and one, passing into a change that turns back and returning again.” To this too it is plain from what has already been said that the nature is common not only to the bodies listed before but also to the “heavenly” ones (1 Corinthians 15:40). And if this is so, it is plain that on his view (though I do not know whether in truth as well) the nature of all bodies is one, passing into a change that turns back and returning again.

It is plain, too, that this is so on the view of those who make the world perishable. But those who do not make it perishable, and who at the same time do not admit a “fifth body”, will also try to show that on their view too the nature of all bodies is one, passing into a change that turns back and returning again. In this way even what perishes persists, passing into change. For the substrate, matter, persists when the quality perishes, according to those who hold that matter is uncreated.

If, however, some argument can show that matter is not uncreated but has come into being for some purpose, it is plain that it will not have the same nature as regards permanence as it would have if it were supposed uncreated. But it is not our present business, as we meet Celsus’s charges, to treat these questions of natural philosophy.

title: Is nothing born of matter immortal?
english: He says also that “nothing born of matter is immortal.” To this it will be said that, if nothing born of matter is immortal, then either the whole world is immortal and is not something born of matter, or the world itself is not an immortal thing either.

If, then, the world is immortal, which is the view even of those who said that only the soul is God’s work and who say that it came from a mixing bowl (Plato, Timaeus 41d), let Celsus show that the world did not come into being from matter without qualities, if he is to keep his saying that “nothing born of matter is immortal.” But if, since the world is born of matter, the world is not immortal, is the world then mortal, and does it perish, or not? For if it perishes, it will perish as a work of God. Then, when the world perishes, what will the soul, the work of God, do? Let Celsus tell us.

But suppose he twists the notion of “immortal” and says that the world is immortal by being perishable and yet not perishing, as being capable of death but not in fact dying. Then plainly, on his view, there will be something at once mortal and immortal, by being capable of both; there will be a mortal thing that does not die; and what is not immortal by nature will be called immortal in a special sense, because it does not die. In what sense of the word, then, will he be drawing his distinction when he says that “nothing born of matter is immortal”? And you see that the ideas in his writings, when they are pressed and put to the test, are shown up as admitting nothing sound and beyond dispute.

After saying this he adds: “On this subject so much is enough; and if anyone is able to hear and inquire further, he will know.” Let us then, who are without understanding in his view, see what has come of our being able to hear him and inquire even a little.

title: Celsus misreads Plato on the amount of evil
english: After this he thinks that we can learn, from a few little phrases, what has been inquired into in many ways about the nature of evils, through many arguments not to be lightly dismissed, and has been interpreted in different ways. He says: “Evils in the things that exist could become neither fewer nor more, in the past, now, or hereafter. For the nature of the whole is one and the same, and the origin of evils is always the same.”

This too seems to have been paraphrased from what is in the Theaetetus, where Socrates in Plato says: “But it is not possible for evils to perish from among men, nor for them to be established among the gods” (Plato, Theaetetus 176a), and what follows. And it seems to me that the man who encompasses the truth in this one treatise, and gives his book against us the title True Doctrine, has not even listened to Plato carefully.

For the passage in the Timaeus that says, “When the gods cleanse the earth with water” (Plato, Timaeus 22d), has shown that the earth, when it is cleansed by the waters, has fewer evils than in the time before it was cleansed. And we say, following Plato, that evils are at times fewer, because of the passage in the Theaetetus that says that “evils” cannot “perish from among men.”

title: Evils are not fixed in number
english: I do not know how, while he posits providence, at least so far as the words of this book go, he says that evils are neither more nor fewer but, as it were, fixed. In this he does away with a most excellent doctrine, that vice is without bounds and that evils are by their very definition without limit.

And from his claim that evils have been, are, and will be neither fewer nor more, it seems to follow that things stand as they do on the view of those who hold that the world is imperishable. On their view the balance of the elements comes from providence, which does not allow any one of them to gain the upper hand, so that the world may not perish. In the same way some providence, as it were, stands over the evils, which happen to be just so many, so that they become neither more nor fewer.

Celsus’s argument about evils is refuted in another way too, from the philosophers who have examined the questions of good and evil, and from history. They have shown that at first courtesans hired themselves out to any who wished, outside the city and wearing masks. Later, growing scornful, they laid the masks aside; and since the laws did not allow them to enter the cities, they stayed outside them. But as corruption grew greater day by day, they dared to enter even the cities. Chrysippus says this in his Introduction to Goods and Evils.

From this one may gather, as a case of evils becoming more and fewer, that the men called “two-way men” once stood out in public, taking both the passive and the active part and slaves to the lusts of those who came in to them, and that later the market officials drove them out. And about countless things that have come into human life from vice as it spread abroad, one may say that formerly they did not exist. The most ancient histories, at any rate, though they accuse sinners of countless things, know nothing of those who practise unspeakable vices.

title: One nature does not mean a fixed amount of evil
english: From these things and others like them, how can Celsus fail to look ridiculous when he thinks that evils could never become more or fewer? For even if the nature of the whole is one and the same, it does not at all follow that the origin of evils too is always the same.

For take a particular man. His nature is one and the same, yet things are not always the same with his ruling part, his reason and his actions. At one time he has not yet taken on reason; at another he has taken on vice along with reason, and this vice spreads further or less far. And there are times when he has been turned toward virtue and advances further or less far; and sometimes he even reaches virtue itself, which is found in more contemplations or in fewer.

So it is possible to say all the more of the nature of the whole that, even if it is one and the same in kind, the same things, or things of the same kind, do not always happen in the whole. For there are not always good harvests, nor always failed ones, nor always heavy rains, nor always droughts. So, too, the plenty or the dearth of better souls is not fixed, nor is the spread of worse souls, further or less far.

Indeed, for those who wish to examine everything as precisely as they can, the account of evils is necessary: evils do not always remain in the same state, because of providence, which either preserves what is on earth or cleanses it with floods and conflagrations; and perhaps not only what is on earth but also what is in the whole world, which needs cleansing whenever vice grows great in it.

title: Why the origin of evil is hard to know
english: After this Celsus says: “What the origin of evils is, is not easy to know for one who has not studied philosophy. But it is enough to say to the multitude that evils are not from God, but cling to matter and have their home among mortals. The cycle of mortal things is alike from beginning to end, and by the appointed revolutions it must be that the same things always have been, are, and will be.”

Celsus says that the origin of evils is not easy to know for one who has not studied philosophy. He speaks as though the man who studies philosophy could know their origin easily, while the man who does not cannot easily see the origin of evils, yet can know it, even if only with toil. But to this too we say that the origin of evils is not easy to know even for one who has studied philosophy. Perhaps it is not possible even for such men to know it clearly, unless by the inspiration of God it is made plain what evils are, and shown how they came to exist, and understood in what way they will be done away with.

At any rate, ignorance about God is itself among evils, and the greatest evil is not to know the way to serve God and to show Him reverence. Certainly, even according to Celsus, some of those who studied philosophy did not know this, as is plain from the different schools in philosophy. But according to us, no one will be able to know the origin of evils who has not recognised that it is an evil to think that reverence for God is kept safe in the laws established in states as they are commonly understood.

Nor will anyone be able to know the origin of evils who has not grasped what concerns the one called the devil and his angels (Matthew 25:41): who this one was before he became the devil, how he became the devil, and what caused those called his angels to fall away with him. Whoever is to know this origin must also have understood more precisely about demons: that they are not God’s handiwork in so far as they are demons, but only in so far as they are rational beings of some kind; and from what cause they have come to be such that their ruling part came to exist in the condition of demons. If, then, any other subject among human questions needing examination is hard for our nature to track down, the origin of evils may be counted among these.

title: Evil lies in the ruling part, not in matter
english: Then, as though he had something more secret to say about the origin of evils but kept silent about it and said only what suits the multitude, he says that it is enough to say to the multitude about the origin of evils that “evils are not from God, but cling to matter and have their home among mortals.”

Now it is true that evils are not from God. For according to our Jeremiah too it is plain that “out of the mouth of the Lord will not come forth evil things and the good” (Lamentations 3:38). But it is not true, in our view, that matter, having its home among mortals, is the cause of evils. For the ruling part of each person is the cause of the vice that exists in it, and this vice is what is evil; and the actions that come from it are evils too. And in our view, speaking strictly, nothing else is evil.

But I know that this subject needs much working out and proof. These can come, by the grace of God who enlightens the ruling part, to the one whom God has judged worthy of the knowledge of this subject too.

title: If all things recur, nothing is in our power
english: I do not know how Celsus, writing against us, thought it useful to toss in a doctrine that needs a great deal of proof, even if only plausible proof, to establish as far as possible that “the cycle of mortal things is alike from beginning to end, and according to the appointed revolutions it is necessary that the same things always have been, are, and will be.” If this is true, what lies in our power is abolished.

For if “according to the appointed revolutions it is necessary that the same things always have been, are, and will be” in the cycle of mortal things, then clearly Socrates must always practise philosophy and always be accused on the charge of new divinities and of corrupting the young; Anytus and Meletus must always accuse him; and the council on the Areopagus must always vote to condemn him to death by hemlock. In the same way, according to the appointed cycles, Phalaris must always rule as a tyrant, Alexander of Pherae must always commit the same cruelties, and those condemned to Phalaris’s bull must always bellow inside it. If this is granted, I do not know how what lies in our power will be kept safe, or how praise and blame will be reasonable.

Against such a hypothesis this will be said to Celsus: if the cycle of mortal things is always alike from beginning to end, and according to the appointed revolutions it is necessary that the same things always have been, are, and will be, then according to the appointed cycles Moses must always go out of Egypt with the people of the Jews, and Jesus must come again to dwell in this life to do the same things that he has done, not once but countless times, cycle after cycle. Indeed, the same Christians too will exist in the appointed revolutions, and Celsus will write this book again, having written it countless times before.

title: The Stoic doctrine of worlds that return
english: Celsus, then, says that only the cycle of mortal things, according to the appointed revolutions, by necessity always has been, is, and will be. But most of the Stoics say that it is not only the cycle of mortal things that is of this kind, but also that of immortal beings and of those they hold to be gods. For after the conflagration of the universe, which has happened countless times and will happen countless times, the same order of all things from beginning to end has come about and will come about.

Yet the men of the Stoa, trying somehow to remedy the absurdities, say, I do not know how, that in each cycle all will be indistinguishable from those of the earlier cycles, so that it is not Socrates who comes into being again but someone indistinguishable from Socrates, who will marry a woman indistinguishable from Xanthippe and be accused by men indistinguishable from Anytus and Meletus. But I do not know how the world is always the same, and not one world indistinguishable from another, while the things in it are not the same but indistinguishable.

However, the principal argument against both Celsus’s words and those of the Stoa will be examined more suitably elsewhere, since at the present time, and for the task now before us, it is not fitting to dwell at length on these matters.

title: God tends a changing world like a farmer through the seasons
english: After this he says: “Nor have the things that are seen been given to man; but each thing comes into being and perishes for the sake of the preservation of the whole, according to the exchange I spoke of before, from one into another.” It is superfluous to spend more time refuting this, since we have already set out the refutation as best we could.

A reply has also been given to this: “Neither good things nor evil things among mortals could become fewer or more.” And we have spoken as well to this: “Nor does God need a new correction.” But God does not, like a man who has built something defectively and made it with too little skill, apply a correction to the world when he cleanses it by a flood or a conflagration. Rather, he is checking the outpouring of evil so that it spreads no further; and I think that he is also doing away with it altogether, in due order, to the benefit of the whole. Whether, after evil has been done away with, there is reason for it to come into being again or not, such questions will be examined in a discussion devoted to them.

So God does indeed always will to repair faults by a new correction. For even if everything was ordered by him in the most beautiful and most secure way in the making of the universe, he nonetheless needed a kind of healing art for those sick with evil and for the whole world, which evil has, as it were, defiled. And nothing has been neglected by God, or will be neglected, since at each time he does what it was fitting for him to do in a world that is changeable and subject to alteration.

And just as a farmer does different kinds of farm work on the land and on what grows from it according to the different seasons of the year, so God orders whole ages as if they were, so to speak, years, doing in each of them whatever the reasonable order of the universe itself requires, which God alone grasps most clearly, as it truly is, and carries out.

title: The wicked serve the whole but remain to blame
english: Celsus has put forward an argument of this kind about evils: “Even if something seems evil to you, it is not yet clear whether it is evil; for you do not know what benefits you, or another, or the whole.” The argument has something cautious in it, but it also suggests that the nature of evils is not altogether wicked, because what is thought to be evil in particular cases may benefit the whole.

Nevertheless, so that no one may mishear what is said and find in it an occasion of ruin, as though his wickedness too were useful to the universe, or at least could be useful, this will be said: since what lies in each person’s power is kept safe, even if God makes use of the wickedness of the bad for the ordering of the universe, assigning them to a use for the universe, such a person is no less blameworthy, and it is as one blameworthy that he has been assigned to a use that every individual would pray to escape but which is useful to the whole.

It is as if, in the case of cities, someone were to say that a man who had committed certain crimes, and for those crimes was condemned to certain public works useful to the community, does something useful for the whole city, while he himself has come into a wretched state, one in which no one with even a moderate amount of sense would want to be.

Paul too, the apostle of Jesus, teaches us that even the very worst will contribute something to the use of the universe, but will through their own fault be in a wretched state, and that the most virtuous will also be most useful to the universe and, through their own doing, will be set in the finest place. He says: “In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and of clay, some for honour and some for dishonour. If anyone, then, cleanses himself, he will be a vessel for honour, sanctified and useful to the master, prepared for every good work” (2 Timothy 2:20–21).

I take it that these things too had to be set out in answer to “Even if something seems evil to you, it is not yet clear whether it is evil; for you do not know what benefits you or another,” so that no one may take from what is said on this subject an occasion for sinning, as though he will be useful to the whole through his sin.

title: Scripture speaks to us as we speak to children
english: After this Celsus, failing to understand them, ridicules the passages in the Scriptures that speak of God as though he were subject to human passions, the passages in which words of wrath are spoken against the ungodly and threats against those who have sinned. To this we must say: just as we, when we talk with very young children, do not aim in our speech at the full measure of our own ability, but adapt ourselves to the weakness of those in our charge and say, and also do, what seems to us useful for turning the children back and correcting them, as children, so the Word of God seems to have arranged what has been written, measuring what was fitting in the telling by the capacity of the hearers and by what would be useful to them.

And in general, about this manner of speaking of God, it is said in Deuteronomy: “The Lord your God bore your ways, as a man might bear the ways of his son” (Deuteronomy 1:31). Bearing, as it were, the ways of a man for the benefit of human beings, the Word says such things. For the many did not need God, where he is represented as speaking, to say what was to be said to such people in a way befitting himself.

But whoever cares about the clear meaning of the divine writings will find from them the things that are called spiritual for those who are called spiritual (1 Corinthians 2:13), comparing the intent of what is said to the weaker with that of what is announced to the more advanced, since both often lie in the same expression for anyone who knows how to hear it.

title: God’s wrath is discipline, not passion
english: We do, then, speak of the wrath of God; but we say that it is not a passion of his. It is something employed to discipline, by sterner methods, those who have committed sins so many and of such a kind. That what is called the wrath of God, and what is named his anger, disciplines, and that this is the teaching of the Word, is clear from what is said in the sixth Psalm: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath” (Psalm 6:1); and in Jeremiah: “Discipline us, Lord, but with judgment and not in anger, lest you make us few” (Jeremiah 10:24).

And anyone who reads in the second book of Samuel of the “wrath” of God that moved David to number the people (2 Samuel 24:1), and in the first book of Chronicles of “the devil” (1 Chronicles 21:1), and compares the texts with each other, will see to whom the wrath is to be assigned. Paul says that all human beings have become “children” of this wrath, in the words: “We were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Ephesians 2:3).

That wrath is not a passion of God, but that each person prepares it for himself through his sins, Paul will make plain where he says: “Or do you despise the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness is leading you to repentance? But by your hardness and your unrepentant heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God” (Romans 2:4–5). How then can each person “store up wrath for himself on the day of wrath” if “wrath” is understood as the passion? And how can a passion of wrath discipline? Moreover, the Word that teaches us never to be angry at all, and says in the thirty-sixth Psalm, “Cease from wrath, and forsake anger” (Psalm 37:8), and says also in Paul, “You too, put away all these: wrath, anger, malice, slander, foul talk” (Colossians 3:8), would not fasten on God himself the passion from which it wishes to free us entirely.

That what is said about the wrath of God is meant figuratively is clear also from the fact that sleep is recorded of him. As if waking him from it, the prophet says: “Rise up; why do you sleep, Lord?” (Psalm 44:23). And again he says: “And the Lord awoke like one who sleeps, like a mighty man reeling from wine” (Psalm 78:65). If, then, sleep means something else, and not what the obvious reading of the words shows, why should wrath not be understood in a similar way too?

The threats, moreover, are announcements of what will befall the wicked. It is as if someone were to call the words of a physician threats as well, when he says to his patients: “I will cut you and apply cauteries to you if you do not obey my rules and keep to this diet and conduct yourself in this way.”

We, then, do not attach human passions to God, nor do we hold impious opinions about him; nor do we go astray when we set out the accounts about him from the Scriptures themselves, compared with one another. And those among us who act with understanding as ambassadors of the Word have no other aim than to free their hearers from simple-mindedness as far as they can, and to make them wise.

title: The wrath the Jews stored up, and Celsus’s boast about all nature
english: In keeping with his failure to understand what is written about the wrath of God, he says: “Is it not laughable that a man, angered at the Jews, destroyed them all, young and old, and burned them out, so that they came to nothing, while God the greatest, as they say, being angry and wrathful and threatening, sends his Son, and he suffers such things?”

Well then, if the Jews, after doing to Jesus what they dared to do against Him, perished young and old and were burned out, they suffered these things from no other wrath than the one they stored up for themselves (Romans 2:5). The judgment of God against them, which came about by God’s appointment, is called “wrath” by a certain ancestral usage of the Hebrews. And the Son of the greatest God does indeed suffer, by His own will, for the salvation of human beings, as we have said above as far as we were able.

After this he says: “But so that the argument may not be about the Jews only (for that is not what I am saying), but about the whole of nature, as I promised, I shall make what I said before clearer.” Who, being modest and aware of human weakness, could read these words and not shrink from the offensiveness of a man who promised to give an account of the whole of nature, and who boasted just as he did in the title he dared to set on his book? Let us see, then, what it is that he promises to say about the whole of nature, and what he promises to make clear.

title: Providence cares first for rational beings
english: Next, at great length, he charges us with saying that God made all things for man. And he wants to show, from the natural history of animals and the shrewdness that shows itself in them, that all things have come into being no more for the sake of human beings than for the sake of the irrational animals. He seems to me to say something like those who, out of enmity toward those they hate, accuse them of the very things for which their own dearest friends are praised. For just as with these, hatred blinds them so that they do not see that they are accusing even their dearest friends by the very things through which they think they are speaking ill of their enemies, so in the same way Celsus too, his reasoning thrown into confusion, has not seen that he is also accusing the philosophers of the Stoa. They rightly set man, and in a word the rational nature, above all irrational things, and they say that providence made all things primarily for its sake. And the rational beings, which come first, stand in the place of children being born, while the irrational and the lifeless stand in the place of the afterbirth that is formed along with the child.

And I think that, just as in cities those who look after the goods for sale and the market look after them for no other reason than for the sake of human beings, yet dogs too and others of the irrational animals have a share in the plenty, so providence takes thought primarily for rational beings, and it has followed that the irrational animals also enjoy what is made for human beings. And just as a man is wrong who says that the market officers look after human beings no more than dogs, since the dogs too share in the plenty of the goods for sale, so much more do Celsus and those who think as he does commit impiety against God, who takes thought for rational beings, when they say: “Why are these things produced as food for human beings rather than for plants, for trees and grasses and thorns?”

title: Thunder, rain and growing things are the work of providence
english: For first he thinks that thunders and lightnings and rains are not works of God, and here he is already showing himself an Epicurean more openly. Second, he says that even if one should grant that these are works of God, they are produced no more as food for us human beings than for plants, for trees and grasses and thorns. In this, like a true Epicurean, he grants that these things happen by chance and not by providence. For if these things are no more useful to us than to plants and trees and grasses and thorns, it is plain either that they do not come from providence at all, or that they come from a providence that takes no more thought for us than for trees and grass and thorn. Each of these is impious on its face; and to take a stand and argue against such things in reply to a man who accuses us of impiety is foolish, for it is plain to everyone from what has been said who the impious one is.

Then he says: “Even if you say that these things grow for human beings” (he plainly means the plants and trees and grasses and thorns), “why will you say that they grow for human beings rather than for the most savage irrational animals?” Let Celsus, then, say plainly that the great variety of the things that grow on the earth is not the work of providence, but that some chance meeting of atoms made such a great range of qualities, and that it is by chance that so many kinds of plants and trees and grass are like one another; and that no craftsman’s reason gave them their being, nor do they have their origin from a Mind that surpasses all wonder.

But we Christians, who are devoted to the God who created these things, and to Him alone, give thanks for these things too to Him who fashioned them as well, because He has made ready for us so great a home, and for our sake for the animals that serve us: “He makes grass spring up for the cattle, and green plants for the service of men, to bring forth bread from the earth, and that wine may gladden the heart of man, that his face may shine with oil, and that bread may strengthen the heart of man” (Psalm 104:14–15).

And if He has prepared food even for the most savage of the animals, it is no wonder; for others too among those who have pursued philosophy have said that these animals also came into being to give exercise to the rational animal. And one of the wise men among us says somewhere: “Do not say, ‘What is this? What is this for?’ For all things have been created for their use” (Sirach 39:21); and, “Do not say, ‘What is this? What is this for?’ For all things will be sought out in their time” (Sirach 39:17).

title: Why God made man needy
english: Next, Celsus, wishing to maintain that providence made what grows on the earth no more for us than for the most savage of the animals, says: “We, for our part, toiling and labouring hard, feed ourselves barely and with great effort, while for them ‘all things grow unsown and untilled’ (Homer, Odyssey 9.109).” He does not see that God, wishing to exercise human understanding on every side, so that it might not stay idle and never devise the arts, made man needy, so that by his very neediness he might be compelled to find out arts, some for food and others for shelter. For it was better for those who were not going to seek things divine and to pursue philosophy to be in want, so that they would use their understanding to find out arts, than to have plenty of everything and neglect their understanding.

At any rate, the lack of what life needs brought into being farming, vine-dressing and the arts of gardening, and also carpentry and smithing, which make tools for the arts that serve the getting of food. The lack of shelter brought in weaving, which comes after carding and spinning, and also building; and so understanding rose even to architecture. And want of necessities has caused the things produced in other places to be carried, by seafaring and the pilot’s art, to those who do not have them. So for these reasons too one might admire providence, which, for our good, made the rational being needier than the irrational animals. For the irrational animals have their food ready to hand, since they have not even a starting point for the arts; and they have a natural covering, for they are clad with hair or feathers or scales or shells.

Let this, then, be said by us in defence against the passage in Celsus that says: “We, for our part, toiling and labouring hard, barely feed ourselves, while for them ‘all things grow unsown and untilled.’”

title: Euripides on the sun and night that serve mortals
english: Next, forgetting that his aim is to accuse Jews and Christians, he raises against himself an iambic line of Euripides that runs counter to his own view; and, coming to grips with what was said, he charges it with being badly said. Celsus’s words run thus: “And if you quote the line of Euripides, that ‘sun and night serve mortals’ (Euripides, Phoenician Women 546), why do they serve us more than the ants and the flies? For to them too night comes for rest, and day for seeing and working.”

It is clear, then, that not only some of the Jews and Christians have said that the sun and the things in heaven serve us, but also the man whom some call the philosopher of the stage, who had been a hearer of Anaxagoras’s teaching on nature. From one rational being, man, he speaks by synecdoche of all rational beings, and says that the things set in order in the universe serve them; and these things in turn are shown by synecdoche in the words “sun and night.” Or perhaps the tragic poet also called the day “sun”, after the sun that makes the day, teaching that the things which most need day and night are those beneath the moon, and of these none so much as the things on earth.
