Day and “night,” then, “serve mortals,” since they come into being for the sake of rational beings. And if ants and flies, which work by day and rest at night, also have a share in what has come into being for human beings, we must not say that day and night come into being for ants and flies as well, nor that they come into being for nothing; but we must hold that these things came into being by providence for the sake of human beings.

title: Understanding makes man master of the beasts
english: Next he raises against himself what is said as if on behalf of human beings, that the irrational animals were fashioned for their sake. And he says: “If someone should call us rulers of the animals, because we hunt the other animals and feast on them, we shall say: Why were we not rather made for their sake, since they hunt us and eat us? What is more, we need nets and weapons and many men to help us, and dogs, against the beasts we hunt; but to them nature has given weapons at once and of themselves, and easily makes us subject to them.”

And here too you see in what way understanding has been given to us as a great help, stronger than any weapon the beasts seem to have. At any rate we, who are much weaker in body than the animals and very much smaller than some of them, master the beasts by our understanding, and hunt even elephants, huge as they are. Those that are by nature able to be tamed we bring under our own civilised life; and against those that are not, or that do not seem to offer us any use from taming, we take our stand with such security for ourselves that, when we wish, we keep such great beasts shut up, and when we need the food that comes from their bodies, we kill them just as we do the animals that are not wild. So the Creator has made all things servants of the rational animal and of its natural understanding.

We need dogs for some purposes, for example to guard flocks of sheep or herds of cattle or herds of goats, or houses; for others we need oxen, as for farming; and for others we use beasts of burden or animals that carry loads. So too the race of lions and bears and leopards and boars and the like is said to have been given to us to exercise the seeds of courage in us.

title: Men and beasts at the beginning
english: Next, addressing the race of men who perceive their own superiority over the irrational animals, he says: “As for what you say, that God has given us the power to catch wild beasts and make use of them, we shall reply that, in all likelihood, before there were cities and arts and such ways of living together, and weapons and nets, men were carried off and eaten by wild beasts, while wild beasts were very seldom caught by men.”

Observe, in answer to this, that even if men catch wild beasts and wild beasts carry off men, there is a great difference between those who prevail by understanding and the beasts that get the better, by savagery and cruelty, of men who do not use their understanding to keep from suffering anything at the hands of beasts.

And the words “before there were cities and arts and such ways of living together” come, I think, from a man who has forgotten what he said earlier: that the world is unbegotten and indestructible, and that only the things on earth suffer floods and conflagrations, and that not all of them meet with these at once. Just as those who hold that the world is unbegotten cannot speak of its beginning, so neither can they speak of a time when there were no cities at all and the arts had not yet been discovered.

But let us grant him this too; it agrees with our own views, though no longer with his, or with what he said earlier. What has this to do with the claim that at the beginning men were certainly carried off and eaten by wild beasts, while the beasts were not caught by men? For if the world came into being by providence, and God presides over the universe, the first sparks of the human race, when it began, must have come under some protection from higher beings, so that at the beginning there was fellowship between the divine nature and men. The poet of Ascra had this in mind when he said: “For then the feasts were shared, and the seats were shared, by immortal gods and mortal men” (Hesiod, Catalogue of Women, fragment 1.6–7).

title: God watched over the first men
english: The divine account in Moses, too, shows the first men hearing a more divine voice and oracles (Genesis 3:8), and sometimes seeing visits made to them by angels of God (Genesis 18:1–2; 19:1). For it is likely that at the beginning of the world human nature was given more help, until, having made progress in understanding and the other virtues and in the discovery of the arts, men could live on their own as well, without always needing those who serve the will of God to guard and manage them through wondrous appearances.

It follows from this that it is false to say that at the beginning men were carried off and eaten by wild beasts, while wild beasts were very seldom caught by men. From this, then, it is clear that what Celsus says in these words is also false: “So in this respect, at least, it was rather men that God made subject to the beasts.” For God did not make men subject to the beasts. Rather, he granted that the beasts should be caught by human understanding and by the arts against them that arise from understanding. For it was not without God that men contrived for themselves safety from the beasts and mastery over them.

title: Bees and ants do not reason
english: Our noble friend does not see how many philosophers there are, philosophers who bring in providence and say that it makes all things for the sake of rational beings, whose useful doctrines he is doing away with, as far as he can, along with the agreement of Christians with philosophy on these points. Nor does he see how great a harm, one that hinders piety, comes from accepting that in God’s sight man differs in no way from ants or bees. He says: “If men are thought to differ from the irrational animals because they live in cities and have a constitution, offices and governments, this is nothing to the point; for so do ants and bees. Bees, at any rate, have a leader, and they have a following and service, wars and victories and the capture of the defeated, cities and even outskirts, the handing on of work in turn, and penalties against the idle and the wicked; at any rate they drive away and punish the drones.”

Here too he has not seen how what is accomplished by reason and rational thought differs from what comes about from irrational nature and mere physical make-up. For these latter, no reason dwelling within the creatures that do them is responsible, since they have none; rather, the most ancient Word, who is the Son of God and King of all that is subject to him, has made an irrational nature which, being irrational, comes to the help of those not granted reason.

Cities, then, came into being among men together with many arts and an ordering of laws. And the constitutions, offices and governments among men are either those so called in the proper sense, which are certain virtuous dispositions and activities, or those given these names in a looser sense, because they imitate the former as far as they can. For it was by looking to those that successful lawgivers established the best constitutions, offices and governments.

None of these can be found among irrational creatures, even if Celsus carries over to ants and bees the names that belong to reason and are assigned to rational beings: city, constitutions, offices and governments. For these things we must in no way commend the ants or the bees, since they do not act with reasoning. We must rather marvel at the divine nature, which has extended even to irrational creatures something like an imitation of rational beings, perhaps to put rational beings to shame: so that, looking at ants, they may become more industrious and more careful to store up what is useful to them (Proverbs 6:6–8), and, observing bees, they may obey their governments and share out the useful tasks of the commonwealth for the safety of their cities.

title: Man works together with providence
english: Perhaps, too, in what one might call the wars of the bees a lesson is laid up: that wars among men, if ever they must be fought, should be just and orderly. And there are no cities and outskirts among bees; rather, the hives and the six-sided cells, the labours of the bees and the handing on of them among them, exist for the sake of men, who need honey for many purposes, both for treating ailing bodies and as pure food.

Nor should what the bees do against the drones be compared with the penalties against the idle and the wicked in cities and with the punishments inflicted on them. But, as I said before, in these things we must marvel at nature; and we must commend man, who can reason about all things and set all things in order, as one who works together with providence, accomplishing works not of God’s providence alone but also of man’s own.

title: Ants, burdens and the image of God
english: Having spoken of the bees, in order to belittle, as far as he can, the cities, constitutions, offices and governments, and the wars for the fatherland, not of us Christians only but of all men, Celsus next goes on to set out a eulogy of ants. His aim is that by praising them he may overthrow, through his comparison with ants, men’s careful management of their food, and cast down their forethought in providing for winter as having nothing more in it than the irrational foresight he supposes ants to have.

Which of the simpler sort of people, who do not know how to look into the nature of all things, would Celsus not turn aside, as far as he can, from helping those weighed down by burdens and sharing their toils, when he says of ants that “whenever they see one of them tiring, they take up one another’s loads”? For a man who needs the training that comes through reason, and has no understanding of it, will say: “Since, then, we differ in nothing from ants even when we help those who are worn out from carrying very heavy loads, why should we do such a thing to no purpose?”

Ants, being irrational animals, would not be lifted up to think highly of themselves because their works are compared with those of men. But men, who through reason are able to hear how their fellow-feeling is being belittled, would be harmed, as far as it rests with Celsus and his words. He did not see that, in wishing to turn the readers of his book away from Christianity, he also discourages the compassion that even those who are not Christians feel toward people carrying the heaviest of loads. If he had been a philosopher with even some sense of human fellowship, he ought not only to have refrained from destroying, along with Christianity, what is useful among men, but also, if it were possible, to have lent his support to the good things that Christianity holds in common with other men.

And if ants also remove the sprouting parts of the grain they store up, so that it does not swell but lasts them through the year as food, we must not suppose that reasoning in the ants is the cause of this, but nature, the mother of all, which has ordered even irrational creatures, so as to leave not even the smallest thing without some trace of the reason that comes from nature.

Unless, perhaps, Celsus covertly means by this (for in many things he wants to follow Plato) that every soul is of the same kind, and that the soul of a man differs in nothing from that of ants and bees. This is the view of one who brings the soul down from the vault of heaven not into the human body alone, but into the other bodies as well. Christians will not be persuaded by this. They have already learned that the human soul was made “in the image” of God (Genesis 1:27), and they see that it is impossible for a nature fashioned “in the image” of God to wipe out its features entirely and take on others, made after the images of who knows what among the irrational creatures.

title: Do ants hold conversations?
english: Since he also says that the living “set apart a special place for the ants that die, and this serves them as ancestral tombs,” we must reply that the more he speaks in praise of irrational animals, the more, even against his will, he magnifies the work of the Word who set all things in order, and shows the skill that is in men, which can adorn in words even the advantages that irrational creatures have by nature.

But why do I say “irrational”? For Celsus thinks that the creatures which, by the common notions of all men, are called irrational are not irrational at all. At any rate he does not think even ants are irrational, this man who promised to speak about the whole of nature and boasted of truth in the title of his book. For he speaks of ants as conversing with one another, in these words: “And indeed, when they meet one another they converse, and that is why they do not lose their way. So there is among them a full measure of reason, common notions of certain universals, utterance, objects and meanings.”

For one person’s conversing with another takes place in an utterance that makes known some meaning, and often reports about what are called objects. To say that these exist among ants as well, how could that not be the most ridiculous thing of all?

title: The view from heaven
english: And he is not ashamed to add to this, so as to display, even to those who will come after him, how disgraceful his own doctrines are, saying: “Come then, if someone were to look down from heaven upon the earth, how would what we do seem to differ from what ants and bees do?”

Now does the one who, on his supposition, looks from heaven to earth at what men do and what ants do, look at the bodies of men and ants, yet fail to perceive the rational ruling faculty, moved by reasoning, and again the irrational ruling faculty, moved irrationally by impulse and impression together with a certain natural make-up beneath it? But it is absurd that one who looks from heaven at the things on earth should want to look at the bodies of men and ants from so great a distance, and should not much rather see the natures of their ruling faculties and the source of their impulses, whether rational or irrational. And if he once sees the source of all impulses, he would clearly also see the difference, and the superiority of man not only over ants but over elephants too.

For one who looks from heaven will see in irrational creatures, however large their bodies may be, no other principle than, if I may call it so, irrationality; but in rational beings he will see reason, which men share with divine and heavenly beings, and perhaps with the God over all himself. That is why man is said to have been made “in the image” of God (Genesis 1:27); for the “image” of the God over all is his Word (Colossians 1:15).

title: Snakes, eagles, and so-called sorcery
english: Next, as though he were straining to drag the human race still lower and make it like the irrational animals, and wished to leave out nothing recorded of the irrational animals that points to something greater in them, he says that the arts of sorcery are found in some of the irrational animals too, so that men should not pride themselves on this either, as something peculiar to them, nor wish to hold superiority over the irrational animals. He says this: “If men take any pride in sorcery as well, then in this too snakes and eagles are wiser. At any rate they know many antidotes and remedies against harm, and even the powers of certain stones for the safety of their young. If men happen upon these, they think they possess something marvellous.”

First, I do not know how he came to give the name sorcery to the animals’ experience, or some natural grasp, of natural antidotes, for the name sorcery is commonly given to something else; unless, perhaps, as an Epicurean he wishes covertly to discredit all use of such things, as if it belonged to what sorcerers profess. But let it be granted him that men pride themselves greatly on knowing these things, whether they are sorcerers or not. How does it follow that in this respect snakes are wiser than men, because they use fennel to sharpen their sight and quicken their movement? They grasp this single natural thing not by reasoning but from their constitution. Men, however, do not come to such a thing from bare nature, as snakes do, but partly from experience, partly from reason, and sometimes from reflection and by systematic knowledge. So too, even if eagles find the stone called the eagle-stone and carry it to the nest for the safety of the young in it, how does it follow that eagles are wise, and wiser than men, when men found by experience the natural aid given to eagles and, through reasoning, used it with understanding?

title: Animal instinct and the riddles of Proverbs
english: Suppose that other antidotes too are known to the animals. What does this do to show that it is not nature but reason that finds these things in the animals? For if reason were what found them, there would not be found in snakes, in a fixed and limited way, this one thing alone (or say a second and a third as well), and some other thing in the eagle, and so with the rest of the animals; there would be as many as are found among men. As it is, the very fact that the aids are fitted, in a fixed way, to the particular nature of each animal makes it plain that there is no wisdom or reason in them, but a natural constitution suited to such things for the preservation of the animals, a constitution made by the Word.

And yet, had I wished to meet Celsus head on in this matter, I could have used a passage of Solomon from Proverbs, which runs thus: “There are four things that are least upon the earth, but these are wiser than the wise: the ants, who have no strength, who prepare their food in summer; and the rock badgers, a people not strong, who have made their homes in the rocks; the locust has no king, and marches in good order at a single word of command; and the lizard, which leans on its hands and is easily caught, dwells in the strongholds of a king” (Proverbs 30:24–28). But I do not use these words as though their meaning were plain. In keeping with the title (for the book is entitled Proverbs), I search into them as riddles. For it is the custom of these men to divide into many kinds the sayings that show one thing on their face and announce another in a hidden sense, and one of these kinds is the proverb. That is why in our Gospels too it is written that our Saviour said: “These things I have spoken to you in proverbs; the hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in proverbs” (John 16:25). It is not, then, the ants we see that are wiser even “than the wise” (Proverbs 30:24), but those that are signified, as it were, in the form of proverbs. The same must be said of the other animals.

Celsus, however, thinks the books of Jews and Christians utterly simple and unlearned, and supposes that those who interpret them allegorically do so by forcing the intention of the writers. Let Celsus, then, stand refuted by these things too, as one who slanders us to no purpose; and let his argument about snakes and eagles, in which he declared them wiser than men, stand refuted as well.

title: Celsus says the animals are nearer to God
english: Wishing to show at still greater length that even notions about the divine are not the special mark of the human race above all mortal things, and to declare that some of the irrational animals too have notions about God, about whom such disagreements have arisen even among the sharpest of men everywhere, Greeks and barbarians alike, he says: “If man is thought to excel the other animals because he has grasped notions of the divine, let those who say so know that many of the other animals too will lay claim to this. And with very good reason. For what could one call more divine than to foreknow and foretell what is to come? This, then, men learn from the other animals, and above all from birds; and those who understand the signs they give are the diviners. If, then, birds and all the other prophetic animals, having foreknowledge from God, teach us through signs, they seem by so much to be nearer by nature to converse with the divine, and to be wiser and dearer to God. The men of understanding say that these creatures also have converse among themselves, plainly holier than ours, and that they themselves somehow understand what is said and show in deed that they understand: when they have foretold that the birds said they would go off somewhere and do this or that, they show them going there and doing just what they had foretold. And nothing seems to keep its oaths better than the elephant, or to be more loyal toward the divine, surely because elephants have knowledge of it.”

See in these words how many questions disputed among philosophers, not only among the Greeks but also among the barbarians, he snatches up and sets out as agreed. These philosophers either discovered, or learned from certain demons, what concerns omen-birds and the other animals from which, it is said, certain prophecies come to men. For first, it has been asked whether there is any art of augury, and in a word any divination through animals, or not. Second, among those who have accepted that divination through birds exists, there is no agreement on the cause of the manner of the divination. For some say that the animals are moved by certain demons or prophetic gods: birds to different flights and different cries, the others to this or that kind of movement. Others say that their souls are more divine and fitted for this, which is most unconvincing.

title: Should we go to the birds for teachers?
english: Celsus, then, since by these arguments he wished to prove the irrational animals more divine and wiser than men, ought to have established at greater length that such divination exists. After that he ought to have set out its defence more clearly, rejecting with proof the arguments of those who do away with such divinations, and overturning with proof as well the arguments of those who said that the animals’ movements for prophesying come from demons or gods. And after that he ought to have established that the soul of the irrational animals is more divine. Had he done so, and shown a philosopher’s habit of mind on matters so great, we would have opposed his plausible arguments as far as we were able: overturning the claim that the irrational animals are wiser than men, and proving false the claims that they have holier notions of the divine than ours and that they hold some holy converse with one another.

As it is, the man who reproaches us for believing in the God who is over all expects us to believe that the souls of birds have more divine and clearer notions than men. If this is true, birds have clearer notions about God than Celsus has; and it is no wonder that they surpass Celsus, who belittles man to such a degree. But indeed, so far as Celsus is concerned, birds have greater and more divine notions, I do not say than we Christians, or than the Jews who use the same Scriptures as we do, but even than the theologians among the Greeks; for they were men. According to Celsus, then, the race of supposedly prophetic birds has grasped the nature of the divine better than Pherecydes and Pythagoras and Socrates and Plato. Then we ought indeed to go to the birds as our teachers, so that, just as on Celsus’s view they teach us by divination what is to come, so too they may free men from doubting about the divine, by handing on the clear notion of it they have grasped. It follows, then, for Celsus, who thinks birds superior to men, that he should use birds as his teachers, and none of those who have pursued philosophy among the Greeks.

title: Prophetic birds cannot foresee their own danger
english: We, for our part, must say a few things out of many in answer to what is before us, so as to refute his false opinion, ungrateful as it is toward the One who made him. For Celsus too, being “a man” who was “in honour,” “did not understand” (Psalm 49:20). That is why he was not even “compared” (Psalm 49:20) with the birds and the other irrational animals that he thinks prophetic. Instead, yielding them the first place, and going further than the Egyptians, who worship irrational animals as gods, he made himself subject to the irrational animals, and, as far as it lay with him, the whole human race too, as though it thought worse and less about the divine than they do.

First of all, then, let it be asked whether divination through birds and the other animals believed to be prophetic exists or does not exist. For the argument advanced on either side is not easy to despise. On the one hand, it urges us not to accept such a thing, so that the rational creature may not abandon the oracles of demons and use birds in their place. On the other hand, it presents the evidence, attested by many, that many people have been saved from the greatest dangers by trusting divination through birds.

For the present, let it be granted that augury is real, so that even so I may show those already prejudiced in its favour that, even if this is granted, man’s superiority over the irrational animals, even over the prophetic ones themselves, is great and beyond any comparison with them. We must say, then, that if there were in them some divine nature that foreknew the future, and so rich that out of its abundance it could show what is to come even to any man who wished, plainly they would have known their own affairs much sooner. And knowing their own affairs, they would have taken care not to fly up over a place where men had set snares and nets against them, or where archers, taking aim at flying creatures, were loosing arrows at them. Surely eagles too, if they foreknew the plot against their young, whether of snakes that climb up to them and destroy them or of men who take them for sport or for some other use and keeping, would not have nested where they were going to be plotted against. And, in a word, none of these animals would ever have been caught by men, if it were more divine and wiser than men.

title: Homer’s birds and serpents foresaw nothing
english: Moreover, if birds of omen fight with birds of omen, and if, as Celsus says, the prophetic birds and the other irrational animals, having a divine nature, notions of the divine and foreknowledge of the future, foretold such things to others, then Homer’s sparrow would not have nested where a serpent was going to destroy her and her young, nor would the serpent in the same poet have failed to guard against being seized by the eagle.

For Homer, so admirable a poet, says this about the first: “Then a great sign appeared: a serpent, blood-red on its back, terrible, which the Olympian himself sent forth into the light, darted out from beneath the altar and sped to the plane tree. There were the young of a sparrow, helpless nestlings, on the topmost bough, cowering under the leaves, eight of them, and the mother that bore them was the ninth. There it devoured them as they chirped piteously, while the mother fluttered round, wailing for her dear young; then, coiling itself, it caught her by the wing as she shrieked around it. But when it had eaten the sparrow’s young and the mother herself, the god who had shown it made it conspicuous; for the son of crooked-counselling Cronus turned it to stone. And we stood and marvelled at what had come to pass. So, when the dread portents of the gods broke in upon the hecatombs…” (Homer, Iliad 2.308–321).

And about the second he says: “For a bird had come upon them as they were eager to cross, an eagle flying high, skirting the host on the left, bearing in its talons a monstrous blood-red serpent, alive and still writhing; and it had not yet forgotten the fight, for it struck its captor on the breast beside the neck, bending itself backward; and the eagle, stung with pain, flung it from him to the ground and cast it down in the midst of the throng, and itself, with a scream, flew off on the blasts of the wind. And the Trojans shuddered when they saw the glittering snake lying in their midst, a portent of Zeus who bears the aegis” (Homer, Iliad 12.200–209).

Was the eagle, then, prophetic, and the serpent not prophetic, although the augurs use this animal too? What, then? Since the arbitrary choice of one over the other is easily refuted, would not the view that both are prophetic be refuted as well? For if the serpent had been prophetic, would it not have guarded against suffering this from the eagle? One could find countless other examples like these, showing that it is not the animals that have in themselves a prophetic soul. Rather, according to the poet and most men, “the Olympian himself sent it forth into the light” (Homer, Iliad 2.309); and in a certain sign Apollo too uses a hawk as his messenger, for the “falcon” is said to be “Apollo’s swift messenger” (Homer, Odyssey 15.526).

title: Demons work through wild animals
english: In our view, however, certain wicked demons, Titan-like or Giant-like, if I may so name them, who have become impious toward what is truly divine and toward the angels in heaven, and have fallen from heaven, and wallow among the grosser and unclean bodies on earth, have some power of discerning the future, since they are bare of earthly bodies. Occupied with this kind of work and wishing to lead the human race away from the true God, they slip into the more rapacious and wilder animals, and others more cunning, and move them to whatever they wish, whenever they wish; or they turn the imaginations of such animals toward flights and movements of this sort. Their aim is that men, caught by the divination found in irrational animals, may not seek the God who encompasses the universe, nor inquire into the pure worship of God, but may sink in their thinking down to the earth, and to birds and serpents, and besides to foxes and wolves.

For those skilled in these matters have observed that the clearer forecasts come through animals of this kind. The reason is that the demons cannot do as much in the tamer animals as they can work in these, because of the close likeness between wickedness and what is found in such animals, which is not wickedness, but something like wickedness.

title: Why Moses called the prophetic animals unclean
english: Hence, if I have admired anything else in Moses, I will declare this too worthy of admiration. He understood the different natures of animals, and, whether he learned from God about them and about the demons akin to each animal, or found it out himself as he rose by wisdom, in his ordinance concerning animals he said that all those reckoned prophetic by the Egyptians and the rest of mankind are unclean, and that, in general, those not of this kind are clean (Leviticus 11:1–47; Deuteronomy 14:3–20). Among the unclean in Moses are the wolf, the fox and the serpent, the eagle, the hawk and the like (Leviticus 11:13–19, 27, 42; Deuteronomy 14:12–18). And, in general, not only in the Law but also in the Prophets you would find these animals taken as examples of the very worst things, and you would never find a wolf or a fox named in connection with anything good.

It seems, then, that there is a certain fellowship between each kind of demon and each kind of animal. And just as among men some are stronger than others, not necessarily because of their character, in the same way some demons may be more powerful than others in morally indifferent matters. Some of them use these animals to deceive men, according to the will of the one who in our teaching is called “the ruler of this age” (John 12:31; 1 Corinthians 2:6), while others give their forewarnings through another kind. And see how foul the demons are, so that even weasels are used by some to reveal the future.

And you, judge for yourself which is better to accept: that the God over all and His Son move birds and the other animals to divination; or that those who move such animals, and not men, though men are present, are wicked demons, and, as our sacred writings have named them, “unclean” (Matthew 10:1).

title: Omens from men, and sneezing
english: If the soul of birds is divine because the future is foretold through them, must we not rather say, where omens are taken from men, that the soul of those through whom the omens are heard is divine? On such men’s view, then, the “grinding woman” in Homer was a divine being (Homer, Odyssey 20.105–119), when she said of the suitors: “May they dine here now for the last and latest time.” So she was divine, while so great a man as Odysseus, the friend of Homer’s Athena, was not divine; but, understanding the omens spoken by the divine grinding woman, he rejoiced, as the poet says: “And godlike Odysseus rejoiced at the omen” (Homer, Odyssey 20.120).

Now see: if birds have a divine soul and perceive God, or, as Celsus calls it, “the gods”, then plainly we men too, when we sneeze, sneeze from some divinity and prophetic power that is in us, in our soul. For this too is attested by many. That is why the poet says, “And he sneezed as one was praying”; and why Penelope says, “Do you not see that my son sneezed at your words?” (Homer, Odyssey 17.545).

title: God speaks through prophets, not birds
english: What is truly divine does not use irrational animals, nor just any men, for the knowledge of the future, but the holiest and purest souls of men, which it fills with God and makes prophets (Wisdom of Solomon 7:27). Therefore, if anything else in the law of Moses is wonderfully said, sayings like these must also be counted among them: “You shall not practise augury, nor watch birds” (Leviticus 19:26); and elsewhere: “For the nations, whom the Lord your God will destroy from before you, will listen to omens and divinations; but to you the Lord your God has not granted it so” (Deuteronomy 18:14); and then, next, he says: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers” (Deuteronomy 18:15).

And once, when God wished to turn people away from augury through an augur, He caused a spirit in the augur to say: “For there is no augury in Jacob, nor divination in Israel; in due time it will be told to Jacob and to Israel what God will accomplish” (Numbers 23:23).

Knowing these things, and others like them, we wish to keep the commandment spoken in a mystical sense: “Keep your heart with all watchfulness” (Proverbs 4:23), so that none of the demons may set foot on our ruling faculty, and no spirit of the opposing powers may turn our imagination to what it wishes. And we pray that “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God” may shine “in our hearts” (2 Corinthians 4:6), while the Spirit of God dwells in our imagination and shapes in us images of the things of God; since “all who are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God” (Romans 8:14).

title: Foreknowledge is not in itself divine
english: We must know that foreknowing the future is not in every case divine. In itself it is something indifferent, and it falls to bad and good alike. Physicians, at any rate, foreknow certain things from the art of medicine, even if they are bad in character; and so too pilots, even if they are wicked, foreknow signs of weather, violent winds and changes in the air, from a certain experience and observation; and surely no one will say on that account that they are divine, if they happen to be wicked in character.

False, then, is what Celsus says: “What could one call more divine than to foreknow and foretell the future?” False also is the claim that “many animals lay claim to a notion of the divine”; for none of the irrational animals has a notion of God. False also is the claim that the irrational animals are “nearer to converse with the divine”; since even among men those who are still bad, even if they make the utmost progress, are far from converse with the divine.

Only those, then, who are truly wise and genuinely devout are nearer to converse with the divine. Such are our prophets, and Moses, to whom, because of his great purity, Scripture bore witness, saying: “Moses alone shall draw near to God, but the rest shall not draw near” (Exodus 24:2).

title: Are beasts dearer to God than wise men?
english: How impiously the man who charges us with impiety has said that the irrational animals are not only wiser than human nature but also dearer to God! Who would not be repelled on listening to a man who says that the serpent, the fox, the wolf, the eagle and the hawk are dearer to God than human nature? It follows that he must say that, if these animals are dearer to God than men, then plainly these animals are dearer to God than Socrates, Plato, Pythagoras, Pherecydes and the theologians he praised a little earlier.

One might well pray for him, saying: “If these animals are dearer to God than men, may you become dear to God along with them, and be made like those who, on your view, are dearer to God than men.” And let him not suppose that such a wish is a curse. For who would not pray to become in every way like those who he is convinced are dearer to God, so that he too, like them, may become dear to God?

Celsus, wishing the converse of irrational animals to be holier than ours, attributes this account not to ordinary people but to men of understanding. But in truth the men of understanding are the good, for no bad man has understanding. He speaks, then, in this way: “Men of understanding say that these creatures too have converse, plainly holier than ours, and that they themselves somehow know what is said, and show in deed that they are not ignorant of it, when, having foretold that the birds said they would go off somewhere and do this or that, they show them going there and doing what they had already foretold.”

Now in truth no man of understanding has recorded such things, and no wise man has said that the converse of irrational animals is holier than that of men. But if, to examine Celsus’s views, we look at what follows from them, it is plain that on his view the converse of irrational animals is holier than the solemn discourses of Pherecydes, Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato and the philosophers; which on its very face is not only incongruous but utterly absurd.

And even if we were to believe that some, having learned from the inarticulate cry of birds that the birds will go off somewhere and do this or that, foretell it, we shall say that this too has been shown to men in symbols by the demons, with the aim that man should be deceived by the demons and his mind dragged down from heaven and God to earth and to things lower still.

title: Elephants, storks and the phoenix
english: I do not know how Celsus came to hear even of an oath sworn by elephants, and that they are more faithful toward the divine than we are, and have knowledge of God. For I know many wonderful things that are recorded about the nature of this animal and its tameness, but I am not aware that anyone has spoken of an elephant’s oaths. Unless, perhaps, he has given the name of oath-keeping to their tameness, and to the compact, as it were, which they keep with men once they have come under men’s control; and even that is false. For it is recorded, if only rarely, that elephants which seemed tame have turned savage against men and killed people, and for this were condemned to be put to death as no longer of use.

After this he brings in what is recorded about the stork, that it repays its parents’ care and carries food to those who begot it, in order to prove, as he supposes, that storks are more pious than men. To this we must say that storks do this too not from a considered grasp of duty, nor from reasoning, but from nature. The nature that formed them wished to set forth, in animals without reason, an example that could shame men into repaying the kindness of those who begot them. If Celsus had known how great the difference is between doing these things by reason and performing them without reason, by nature, he would not have said that storks are more pious than men.

Further, as though he were standing up for the piety of animals without reason, Celsus brings in the Arabian creature, the phoenix: at intervals of many years it visits Egypt, bringing its father, who has died and been buried in a ball of myrrh, and lays him down where the precinct of the sun is. This too is recorded. But if it is true, it may also be a work of nature. For divine providence has been lavish in setting before men, in the differences among living things as well, the variety in the ordering of what is in the world, a variety that reaches even to the birds; and it has brought into being a certain “only-begotten” creature, so that by this too it might cause men to wonder not at the creature but at the One who made it.

title: All things made for the rational creature
english: Since, then, Celsus adds to all this the words: “So all things have not been made for man, any more than for the lion, or the eagle, or the dolphin, but so that this world, as the work of God, might come to be whole and complete in all its parts. It is for this that all things have been measured out: not for one another, except incidentally, but for the whole. God cares for the whole, and providence never forsakes it; it does not grow worse, nor does God bring it back to himself after a time; nor is he angry on account of men, any more than on account of apes or mice; nor does he threaten these creatures, each of which has received its own lot in its place”, come, let us answer this, if only briefly.

I think I have shown from what was said earlier how all things have been made for man and for every rational being; for it is chiefly for the sake of the rational living being that all things have been created. So let Celsus say that things were not made for man, any more than for the lion or the other creatures he names. We, for our part, will say: the Creator did not make these things for the lion, or the eagle, or the dolphin, but made all things for the sake of the rational living being, and “so that this world, as the work of God, might come to be whole and complete in all its parts.” For we must agree with this, since it is well said. God cares, not, as Celsus thinks, for the whole alone, but beyond the whole, and in a special way, for every rational being. And providence will never forsake the whole. For even if some part of the whole grows worse because the rational being sins, God so orders things as to make a cleansing of it and, in time, to turn the whole back to himself. Nor indeed is he angry on account of apes or mice; but on men, because they have transgressed the starting points that nature gave them, he brings retribution and punishment. These he threatens through the prophets and through the Saviour who came to dwell among the whole human race, so that through the threat those who hear may turn, while those who neglect the words that call them to turn may pay the penalty they deserve. It is fitting for God to impose such penalties, according to his own will and for the good of the whole, on those who need healing and correction of this kind, and so painful.

But since this fourth book has now reached a sufficient length, we will bring our discourse to a close about here. May God grant, through his Son, who is God the Word (John 1:1), and Wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:24), and Truth (John 14:6), and Righteousness (1 Corinthians 1:30), and whatever else the sacred Scriptures say of him when they speak of him as God, that we may begin the fifth book also, for the benefit of those who will read it, and bring it too to a good end, with his Word coming to dwell in our soul.
